Development oyzu run uses the host environment. Integrated oyzu run test profiles produce test-only bundles that disclose host execution; they do not claim captured-build isolation.

Rust checks cover requested-target validation, transitive selection, root-task semantics, selection integrity, cross-target ownership, required report paths, post-hook collection boundaries, local sibling order and cycles visible only after combining build stages. The core captured-build suite exercises a shared custom prerequisite with two consumers, private workspace effects, successful snapshot packages and failure propagation from the producer post-hook. It also exercises explicit selection with an unprovisioned unrelated toolchain, deduplicated requests, exclusions and selected materialization producers. It tests local prerequisites while compilation waits on a foreign task, and a Node consumer requesting a Go-owned task through the materialization scenario. Its checks execute the compiled CLI with real native tools; suite registration alone is not acceptance. See implementation status for revision-specific local and CI evidence. This adds qualified task composition to the existing builders. It does not complete generated-output inference, task caching, matrix expansion, interactive services or tool installation. Use the authored scenarios and their acceptance criteria to track those remaining capabilities.

Host tasks receive the selected project's pinned tool directories on PATH, plus tool environment values such as GOROOT and JAVA_HOME. For example, argv = ["bash", "scripts/test-database.sh"] can invoke the pinned go by name. The tools must already be installed for the matching lock; oyzu run does not install them. Use oyzu install first (or install --frozen --offline with the required cached tools). Bare bash and sh use the shared host-shell lookup. On Windows, Oyzu skips System32 and WindowsApps WSL launchers, looks for a native shell on PATH, then derives Git for Windows' shell from git.exe on PATH, then checks standard Git install locations. A missing native shell fails with the search locations and an explicit-path remedy; it never silently enters WSL. Git Bash/MSYS converts the ordinary Windows PATH at startup, so pinned Windows tools remain available to the script without an Oyzu PATH conversion layer. Linux/macOS keep normal PATH lookup. Shell-string tasks with shell = "bash" or shell = "sh" use the same lookup. The default shell remains PowerShell on Windows and sh on Linux/macOS. Explicit shell executable paths remain caller-selected. This is host development execution; isolated builds use their executor's shell and tool environment.

oyzu run <task> reports configuration/discovery, selected task, pinned tool environment verification, and native execution as work begins. Preparation that has no native output emits a ten-second activity update; execution reports a heartbeat while its child is running. Required tool verification still completes before task launch and is not bypassed to shorten startup. Local tasks inherit stdin, including redirected pipes, in both text and JSON modes. Text-mode tasks without a bundle inherit stdout/stderr directly. Tasks recording a bundle (integrated oyzu run test, including its prerequisites and hooks) instead tee stdout/stderr to the caller's streams and retain the full output in the bundle's numbered dist/logs/*.stdout and *.stderr files. Output is forwarded without waiting for a newline and is not replayed on completion. -q suppresses routine Oyzu progress while preserving child output and logs. For a bundled task that needs real stdout/stderr terminal descriptors, set interactive = true: text mode then inherits those streams directly. Oyzu does not allocate a pseudo-terminal, so this interactive output cannot also be captured; that task's bundle stdout/stderr logs are empty. Ordinary tee capture preserves terminal stdin and live output, but the child's stdout/stderr are pipes, which can change native buffering, color and terminal detection. Required report files are collected in either mode. Use JSON capture when retained output matters more than terminal-dependent interaction. JSON mode keeps stdout as one final result with captured task output and streams structured diagnostics on stderr. Its child stdout/stderr are not terminals, so prompts on those streams are only visible after completion; use text mode for interactive prompting. Tasks with an empty-stdout validation contract also retain captured output so the check remains enforceable. Captured builds and internal probes continue to receive null stdin. PowerShell shell tasks need interactive = true to omit -NonInteractive; an explicit argv is passed as authored. Inherited native streams retain the child's own color and control-byte behavior, including its handling of NO_COLOR. For example, with a discoverable project and a provisioned POSIX shell, a task argv = ["sh", "-c", "read x; printf 'got:%s\\n' \"$x\""] can consume printf 'hello\n' | oyzu run ask -q and print got:hello. On Windows, use a provisioned native command or PowerShell task appropriate to that shell. An EOF or native input error remains the child's result; Oyzu does not synthesize input or restart the task. This stream change does not add remote terminal forwarding or service supervision. Host process completion wakes the coordinator through a waiter immediately; there is no mandatory 50 ms completion delay. The 50 ms maintenance wakeup remains for captured log following and cooperative cancellation, and heartbeats remain ten seconds. Wait/launch failures remain execution errors and trigger best-effort termination where a child exists. No task speedup numbers are available yet. Regressions cover piped input, live tee output, successful and failed bundle logs, the interactive capture exception and Unix terminal descriptors. See verification status and Windows lifecycle qualification for the platforms and stream scenarios actually checked. Native tools can still buffer their own output; Oyzu's heartbeat is not a claim that a silent tool is making measurable progress. Exit codes and task arguments remain unchanged by presentation.

Each local oyzu run <task> command, prerequisite and hook on Windows runs in a private, noninheritable kill-on-close job. The native task starts suspended, enters its job, then resumes its verified primary thread. Descendants inherit the job; breakaway is not enabled. Hard-killing the Oyzu controller closes its job handles and stops its task trees, releasing descendant-held ports. Ordinary task completion also terminates remaining descendants before joining output pipes. Tasks must not leave background services running after their command returns; run a service in the foreground for the intended lifetime. This applies to terminal, tee and JSON-captured local tasks. Native stdin, argument/batch handling, exit codes, console membership and Ctrl-C broadcast remain unchanged. The controller is not assigned to its own task job, and existing enclosing jobs remain in force. The job provides process lifetime containment, not filesystem/network isolation or permission to execute. Containment uses local OS APIs and needs no account or network access. Captured build processes, metadata probes and remote tasks retain their separate execution contracts; this repair does not change Unix behavior. Job creation/assignment and primary-thread lookup/resume failures abort launch and kill/reap the owned suspended child. Missing or multiple primary threads fail explicitly; there is no uncontained fallback. TASK_JOB_* and TASK_PRIMARY_THREAD_* diagnostics retain the launch failure details. An incompatible enclosing job or denied OS handle access must be corrected before retrying. Normal cleanup confirms job-wide exit within ten seconds; a failure is reported as TASK_JOB_CLEANUP_FAILED rather than successful completion. An externally killed controller cannot report cleanup evidence itself. The disposable compiled-CLI proof covers hard kill, normal exit and Ctrl-C in text and JSON modes, checking task/child/grandchild exits and loopback port release. See Windows lifecycle qualification for platform, commands and remaining verification limits.

Native builds use the shared logical task planner and bounded dependency scheduler. Independent targets may overlap up to build.jobs; declarations such as depends_on: [api] under builds.web delay web until API's selected stages finish successfully. Failed dependencies block consumers, not unrelated targets. Same-target stages and hooks remain ordered because they share native files. --plan exposes the logical edges without installation or execution; native preparation subsequently resolves exact commands and report contracts into the executable evidence plan. Artifact transfer through materialize is also supported in private host target workspaces, after producer actions and report obligations succeed. Ordering alone still transfers no files.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-help.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Run oyzu --help for a workflow-oriented overview: Develop & build, Project tools, Environment & configuration, Platform and Diagnostics. Common examples follow the options. Use oyzu <command> --help or oyzu help <command> for command-specific arguments and options, including nested commands such as oyzu config set --help. Help works offline without a project, installed tool selection or platform account. Hidden shell hooks stay out of the public command list. Help does not execute the examples, install tools or change project files. oyzu --help oyzu build --help oyzu help config oyzu config set --help oyzu --json --help Help uses cyan headings, green command/option names and yellow placeholders on color-capable terminals. Redirected help is plain text by default. Set NO_COLOR=1 to disable help color or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 to request it explicitly (avoid setting both). These are clap's help-rendering controls; project ui.color does not apply because help runs before project configuration is loaded. With --json, successful help/version requests return unstyled text in output and exitCode: 0. The flag can precede the command or follow a command's --help. For oyzu help <command>, put --json before help. This presentation change does not alter other commands' result/error formats or exit codes. Human layout is not a stable machine-parsing contract. The layout and palette use the same CLI implementation on Windows, macOS and Linux. Windows tests cover root/nested help from an empty directory, complete public command grouping, redirected output, forced color, NO_COLOR and JSON help. See implementation status for evidence and platform limits. This design draws on GitHub CLI's command groups, uv's help navigation and the CLI Guidelines' restrained color guidance. No upstream source or new dependencies are included.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-output.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every public command defaults to readable text and accepts global --json for machine-readable output. DEC-033 and AGENTS.md record this product rule. Output selection never changes policy, configuration, lock contents or exit codes. The CLI design guide is the draft shared standard for mission, guardrails, state meanings, large-repository presentation and review criteria. This reference describes current interfaces, including bounded retained build history. Other target experiences in the guide require their own implementation evidence.

The help masthead uses the compact lowercase oyzu. wordmark. Terminals choose their own fonts; no Segoe UI or point-size claim is made for terminal output. Run oyzu --help for a workflow-oriented overview: Develop & build, Project tools, Environment & configuration, Platform and Diagnostics. The overview includes common examples; oyzu <command> --help or oyzu help <command> shows command-specific arguments and options, including nested commands such as oyzu config set --help. Help works offline without a project, installed tool selection or platform account. Hidden shell hooks stay out of the public command list. oyzu reshim appears under Project tools and refreshes the fixed shim folder and existing activation launchers owned by this frontend. Human output reports the shims folder and recorded commands; --json returns directory and commands. See shim refresh for store selection, Windows prerequisites and recovery. shell groups startup profile install and remove; shim refresh has no nested spelling or alias. Help uses cyan headings, green command/option names and yellow placeholders on color-capable terminals. Redirected help is plain text by default. Set NO_COLOR=1 to disable help color or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 to request it explicitly (avoid setting both). These are clap's help-rendering controls; project ui.color does not apply because help runs before project configuration is loaded. JSON help always contains unstyled text. The layout and palette use the same CLI implementation on Windows, macOS and Linux; native verification is recorded in the implementation status. This design draws on GitHub CLI's command groups, uv's help navigation and the CLI Guidelines' restrained color guidance. No upstream source or new dependencies are included.

oyzu --version identifies the compiled local build, for example: oyzu 0.1.0-local.8aee8560a0ca.dirty (debug; x86_64-pc-windows-gnu; build 1791211857) The suffix records the abbreviated source commit, whether the worktree was dirty when compilation captured its identity, Cargo profile, target triple and build Unix timestamp (seconds since the UTC epoch). SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH overrides that timestamp at compilation for reproducible inputs. Without Git metadata, source identity is explicitly unknown.source-unknown. This is diagnostic identity, not a release version, source attestation or production eligibility claim. All current builds are labelled local, including optimized release-profile builds. Identity is embedded at compile time. Version/help never opens project configuration, starts a worker, runs Git or contacts a service. --version --json uses the existing structured output/exit-code envelope.

A pull changes source; it does not replace an installed executable. oyzu --version reports the identity compiled into the selected executable. Use command -v oyzu in POSIX shells or Get-Command oyzu -All in PowerShell to inspect command routing. Compare it with the project-local binary directly: ./.oyzu/bin/oyzu --version ./.oyzu/bin/oyzu build --output plain On Windows use .\.oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe. oyzu build publishes collected artifacts under dist and promotes executable artifacts into the current project's .oyzu/bin only after a successful native build. Failed builds retain the previous binaries. A direct Cargo compilation through oyzu exec writes Cargo's target output and does not perform that promotion. Do not assume target/debug/oyzu identifies the executable selected by your shell. The repository bootstrap reuses an existing executable; it is not an update command. Activation can prepend the configured project-local .oyzu/bin to PATH; ordinary shell-wrapper commands select the application on PATH, while lifecycle hooks retain the bootstrap frontend. Preserve this architecture when updating: verify the successful build's artifact, promoted binary and selected version before changing any installation. No global bootstrap replacement is required for a project-local build. Native Windows routing qualification is recorded separately from cross-platform source/tests.

Default builds use compact linear progress, preceded by one plan table (targets by stages, or platforms by stages for a single target) shown before work starts; the dashboard remains an explicit option. The old linear preparation/context/stage tables and the per-stage Skipped lines are removed. Routine successes and accepted per-action test details collapse; -v, planning, inspection, history and JSON retain deeper detail. A build prints named sections in a fixed order and omits any that has nothing to say. The title line names the project and, right-aligned, the host platform, local or the CI provider, and fast or full. Every row, the title and the section rules share one width (80 columns, or less on a narrower terminal). ── Prepare ── lists every preparation step as a row (mark, name, detail, duration, and the warning count of the work that raised them). The Tools row summarizes the pinned tools (2 tools pinned · 0 installed now) and lists each beneath it with its version, already installed or installed now, and the detected requirement that needs it (or pinned in oyzu.toml), followed by detected toolchain components and host prerequisites of the selected targets. With several targets the block prints once, when Prepare closes, listing each tool once; a tool whose reason differs between targets shows each reason (detected from …; pinned in … · not detected for <target>). Best-effort detection adds attention rows (yellow !) beneath the tools: ! protoc needed by prost-build · not pinned; add it to oyzu.toml (oyzu pin) (an unpinned detected package tool; core toolchains resolve and lock instead, and a pinned tool is an ordinary detected from Cargo.lock row; no catalog entry; pin or provide it marks an unknown tool), host prerequisite … · not found on PATH, fetches <what> outside the lock (<file>) and detection failed: <reason> · nothing extra detected. They warn and never fail the build; tools.ignore silences a detection, visible only with -v. Rules and patterns: build tool scope. When another build holds the workspace, a Build lock row waits for it (waiting for pid N, started Ns ago) before any other preparation instead of failing; Ctrl-C stops the wait. Routine housekeeping that finishes after Prepare closes (end-of-build cache retention) is shown only when slow, failed or warned, or with -v. In an interactive terminal, work in progress shows under its section heading as one line per step or action with an animated spinner, redrawn several times a second; long status is shortened with … rather than wrapped. Redirected and CI output never redraws: each action prints a start and an end line prefixed with elapsed mm:ss, and the ten-second heartbeat names what is still running. ── Build ── has one row per finished action: mark, target, stage, the command shortened with … to fit the width, executed or reused, and its duration. ── Outputs ── lists artifacts as project-relative paths with sizes; -v and --json keep absolute paths. ── Warnings (N) ── lists each distinct warning once, with its owner (for example docs · npm); it is not repeated inline during the run. The generic NATIVE_WARNING code is hidden in the default view and shown with -v and in JSON, while Oyzu-owned diagnostic codes are always shown. The summary line carries the outcome and counts only the outcomes that happened (2 targets · 1 executed · 1 reused · 235.3s), followed by a dim Details line with the manifest and event paths and the invocation id. The separate Action cache line, the "counts do not estimate time remaining" sentence and the "Check selection unavailable … retained evidence is incomplete" sentence are not part of the default build view; -v adds the Reuse and Cache facts, history keeps the selection caveat, and JSON is unchanged. ── Selection ── prints only when the build is not every declared target: --affected shows what it was compared with (compared with origin/main at 0123456), the changed targets and changed paths, their dependents and the unaffected count; a conservative fallback shows ! Not narrowed with its reason, the recorded code and a fix only when one is known; an explicit request shows requested and required (prerequisites pulled in). ── Plan ── then prints once after it. Rows are targets; columns are the stages the builders declare, in the order format, lint, test, build, package and then any other stage. A cell is run (selected), skip (the builder has the stage but it is not selected or not available) or - (the builder declares no such stage). Below the table, after a blank line, one dim line per distinct skip reason names the stages it covers under a skipped label, and table notes follow under a note label, so neither reads as a table row. A single target built for several platforms (--all-platforms) pivots to one row per platform and says 1 target · N platforms. Above twelve rows, targets with identical stages share a counted row (29 targets) and a note line says so; a narrowed build's trailer reads N of M targets and an affected build adds a why column (changed, uses <target>); -v lists every target. When the table would not fit the terminal width each row becomes a record (cli build run · package -, then its skipped stages on the next line) so no value is lost. The table renders the planner's recorded stage and check-selection facts and does not recompute them; a runs on executor column is not shown because no such fact is recorded. A failed action's Build row reads ✗ … failed <duration> (FAIL without color). After Build, a ── Failure: <target> · <stage> ── section shows the native cause (line breaks kept, terminal controls escaped, the first error context or the last lines written), the exit code, Log with the retained log path, and Next oyzu build <target> re-run only this target. Actions that did not run because a prerequisite failed are blocked (⊘), counted apart from failed; a blocked row says needs <target> · <stage>, only the first three get a row and the rest become + N more blocked · -v lists them. The summary counts only non-zero outcomes (✗ Build failed 1 failed · 12 blocked · 130 succeeded · 4m 02s) and is followed by Details and, for a host build, the note that local binaries were not updated. A preparation failure ends after Prepare with a ── Failure: preparation ── block and no Build section. In a build of more than twelve actions, clean successes fold into one ✓ 91 finished · 78 reused · 13 executed tally (-v lists every action); running, warned, waiting, blocked and failed actions keep their rows, and the Build heading says 143 actions. On a terminal the live pane shows ○ <target> · <stage> waits for <target> · <stage> for queued actions with unfinished prerequisites (at most three, then + N more waiting) and an N of M finished line. -q prints only Failure, Warnings and the summary line. Redirected output is rendered at 100 columns on every host; failure text wraps instead of exceeding it, Windows extended-length (\\?\) prefixes are not shown, and a long log path keeps its tail. Interrupted, --plan and --check builds keep their existing receipts. Redirected output and CI logs are appended, not redrawn: each action prints a .. target stage started line and an end line with its outcome and duration, both led by the elapsed mm:ss, and the ten-second heartbeat reads still running: api build 10s · auth-lib test 12s · 6 waiting. In a narrow terminal or without color every table falls back to records and nothing is dropped. When the selected targets live in more than one top-level directory below the project root (./ for targets at the root), the plan table groups its rows under a dim services/ heading, a prerequisite in another directory shows in a final needs column when it fits, Outputs are listed under their directory, and the summary gains one line per directory (services/ ✓ 2 targets 58.1s, where the time is the sum of that directory's action durations). Identical-stage grouping above twelve rows applies within each directory. A build in a single directory is unchanged. With color, state is a glyph (✓ ok, ↺ reused, ! warning, ✗ failed). Without color (NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, redirected output) every mark becomes a padded word (ok, reused, warn, FAIL) and headings use -- Name ---, so no state depends on color. -q prints only warnings and the summary line (failures keep their existing receipt). The titles, rows and receipt are produced by the shared presentation and logging layer; JSON stdout, JSON events and exit status are unchanged. Build receipts include separate target/action totals and nonzero disjoint action outcomes, fresh tests, reused test evidence, warnings and available evidence references. Receipts distinguish captured checks selected (with their action outcomes) from checks not requested. Selection comes from the executed graph's retained target facts, including required checks in fast mode; a fast/full label or missing report never establishes that tests were not requested. A native report with an explicit zero total is labeled Native zero-test reports; native skips keep their own counts. Missing numeric facts display unavailable, not zero. Legacy records without captured selection say Check selection unavailable in history and failed receipts. Required report validation still fails the build, and a successful build does not itself establish release eligibility. Selected history uses the same labels. Successful target totals remain separate from actions labeled executed or reused. Expanded build --explain and selected history retain recorded selection and reuse decisions, source comparison context when available, native provenance and explicit uncertainty; they do not recompute causes from the current checkout. Ordinary misses remain ordinary execution, while material fallback warnings and required failures keep their existing visibility and exit semantics. Successful receipts say Build succeeded, including with warnings when warning diagnostics are present. Native warnings are listed once in the Warnings section, and both human views share compiler/test output projection; raw native records remain in JSON events and retained logs. Intentional stage skips use neutral grouped reasons; missing required work still receives attention. Lifecycle records use compact spacing and a simpler nested description at narrow widths; source excerpts preserve native indentation rather than repeated columns. invocationId correlates a build result with its live and retained events; runId remains the producing build identity. oyzu history lists up to twenty retained build summaries; oyzu history <invocation-or-run-id> --json is a bounded agent-readable result with causes and evidence availability. See retained invocation lookup for scope, limits, access and retention. This does not create an agent-only output mode or a general history service for every command. oyzu pin --dry-run oyzu pin --dry-run --json oyzu --json config show oyzu tools inspect-lock --json oyzu --json tools resolve --registry registry.yaml --tool hashicorp/terraform --version v1.16.5 oyzu exec --json -- ./my-program argument The flag works before or after the subcommand. Arguments after -- belong to the invoked task/program, so its own --json does not select Oyzu's output mode. Inspection, configuration and discovery use titled, indented human views; pin shows a concise requirement inventory. Builds retain their progress and receipt, task lists retain readable labels, and which prints the selected path. All human diagnostics use the shared status/subject/message renderer, including env -v, which -v and shell/payload commands. The old severity/target/timestamp logger envelope and separate build timeline renderer are removed. Verbosity expands observations within the same design. Multiline causes keep their line boundaries. Lookup and payload diagnostics are append-only and create no preparation spool, redraw worker or cursor controls; their stdout contracts (selected paths, environment data and shell code) are unchanged. Plain command views render events without a background redraw worker. Build views retain their ten-second progress heartbeat; interactive builds redraw at up to ten frames per second. Closing either timed build view wakes its wait immediately, so command completion does not wait for the next redraw or heartbeat. oyzu build --verify-contract adds a Contract check block after the Outputs of the final receipt: the outcome (passed, failed, nothing to verify), how many confined actions ran again with their whole target visible, how many matched, diverged or were not confined, and one Diverged row per mismatch naming the extra files and the declaration that fixes them. The same data is manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-verification"] in --json; a divergence is also an error diagnostic and a non-zero exit. A confined action's undeclared read is the diagnostic confined-read-outside-contract with the stage, path, missing fact and fix as indented lines (plain text; no color is needed to read it). See Local action cache.

This section is the normative style guide for every public command's human experience: startup, progress, subprocess output, results and failures. Command-specific presenters must follow it; a generic recursive data dump or raw diagnostic envelope is not a finished public interface. These are review requirements, not a claim that all existing commands have been audited. Lead with the outcome and relevant selection (such as the active profile). Use short, descriptive section headings and aligned columns for comparable records. Keep empty collections compact ([] for configuration values); omit empty diagnostic sections. Do not omit failures or unresolved requirements. Preserve identifiers exactly: env.CARGO_HOME, env._.path, checks.coverageMinimum and cargo-llvm-cov are copyable identifiers, not prose. Never title-case, split capitals, or replace their underscores and punctuation. Humanize only labels owned by the presenter. Group configuration settings by namespace, retaining full setting keys. Render booleans as true/false in configuration tables to match their authored types. Put long identities and low-priority metadata after the useful settings. Wrap long cells without losing characters; use labeled records on narrow terminals. Normalize Windows extended-path notation for human display, while preserving machine payloads. Use cyan headings, green success, yellow attention and red failures. Always include textual meaning; color cannot be the only signal. Preserve readable no-color output, escape terminal controls, and honor each command's redaction contract. Presentation must not recover upstream-redacted values. Verify the compiled command in human, no-color and JSON modes. Cover long identifiers and narrow layouts with focused rendering checks. JSON schemas and executable/native payloads are independent of presentation. Human output leads with the operation outcome, then groups details into named sections. Comparable records use aligned tables; nested or long records use labeled fields without dropping values. The shared renderer uses terminal width when available (100 columns otherwise), falling back to labeled records when a table would overflow. Color is supplementary: headings use cyan, success uses green and attention uses yellow; errors retain explicit severity labels. Shared result views enable color on terminals, omit it for redirected output or TERM=dumb, accept nonzero CLICOLOR_FORCE to force color, and let NO_COLOR override forcing. No project configuration is opened solely to style a result. JSON never gains ANSI sequences. Shell code, native streams and which path output retain their payload contracts. Untrusted control characters in shared human result values are escaped before styling. pin shows one compact setup table per target. For Rust it lists each compiler component and test/coverage helper separately, with a purpose column. Formatting, linting, testing and coverage tools are required when those checks are enabled by the build or policy; the labels do not make selected checks optional. Installation support is distinct from installed availability: pin does not probe or install tools. Sources, profiles, compatibility constraints, configured requests and discovery limitations remain in --json, rather than repeated human tables. Unknown requirements remain visible. Existing resolution-conflict diagnostics are unchanged. Preview/pinned outcomes distinguish completed and incomplete resolution. Incomplete resolution includes actionable diagnostics below the setup table. Environment inspection and shell-profile receipts also use the shared layout.

Command behavior Required human presentation Quick lookup (which, version) Preserve its concise documented payload; no artificial progress or decorative wrapper Inspection/listing (env, config, tools current/list/versions/info, tools resolve, tools evidence, task list, pin preview) Descriptive title, useful selection context, grouped tables or labeled records, actionable unresolved items Work (install, update, build, acquisition) Operation heading, named live steps, scoped subprocess output, final outcome/receipt Task/child execution (run, exec) Shared Oyzu preparation/progress; preserve the documented native stream/pass-through behavior Failure Failed operation and affected item, readable cause, recovery when known; preserve exit status and diagnostic code. A build summary shows each failed action's cause as an ERROR line even when the task never started (for example a rejected artifact handoff); text quoting native tools has its terminal controls escaped and its line breaks kept Shell code/private protocols Exact executable/protocol payload; never add human decoration Consistency means shared hierarchy, vocabulary and state semantics, not adding identical headings to payload commands. Select the pattern in the CLI presenter before starting effects. Application commands return outcomes and lifecycle facts; they do not select colors, terminal modes or human/JSON formatting.

Before potentially slow work, show the operation and what is currently being checked or performed. Do not delay all feedback until the final result. Immediate lookups need no synthetic progress. Name the item or step (rust, Dependencies, Source evidence), not an internal scope such as command or a repeated generic build label. Context statements belong in subtitles or explanatory text; do not make them look like work items. Use one shared state vocabulary: › running, ✓ completed/ready, ✗ failed, ! attention, and explicit Skipped, Blocked, or Unresolved labels. Starting verification is not completion. Mark ready only after the owning operation confirms its required checks. Close started steps on failure as well as success; never leave an apparently running step in a completed receipt. Use elapsed/still-working feedback for genuinely long operations. Use a percentage only when the operation supplies a meaningful total. Do not invent progress or claim stalled work is healthy merely because a heartbeat exists. Keep the default linear. Small redraws may update active rows and bounded subprocess tails on capable terminals; persistent panes, alternate screens and interactive input must not be prerequisites for ordinary use. Group concurrent work by stable target/task/tool identity. Indent and dim each captured subprocess tail beneath its owner, allowing about eight lines subject to the shared terminal budget. Collapse successful tails; retain relevant failure context. Never merge unattributed lines from parallel processes. Native pass-through commands retain their documented stream contract. Finish with a concise outcome and useful results, artifacts or recovery steps. Avoid repeating the complete progress history in the receipt. Partial success, failed verification and missing requirements must remain visible. Routine human progress must not default to envelopes such as [Info] [oyzu::commands] [00:00.045] [command]. Subsystem identifiers, timestamps and diagnostic metadata belong in explicitly requested diagnostic detail and structured logging. Warnings/errors still explain severity and retain useful codes; do not suppress them to make a display look clean. Illustrative shared lifecycle (values are examples, not measured output): Installing tools › rust Checking pinned installation… ✓ rust Ready · 1.95.0 · reused › cargo-nextest Installing… Downloading package… ✓ cargo-nextest Ready · installed Installation complete 2 tools verified · 1 installed · 1 reused The live terminal may replace the running rows; a redirected stream keeps a readable start/completion sequence. Both must communicate the same outcome.

Use the shared renderer's semantic palette and color controls above. Never add command-local ANSI strings or a second styling policy. Dim native previews, not essential status or recovery instructions. When terminal capabilities are absent, use append-only text with no cursor controls; disabling color alone must not remove information. Forced color may style redirected output without enabling redraws. Handle narrow widths without truncating copyable identifiers or paths. Keep progress/diagnostics on stderr and final results on stdout. Preserve the JSON, shell-payload and native-stream exceptions documented below. Quiet removes routine progress, not results or failures; verbosity adds diagnostics without changing execution. Preserve legitimate values under the owning sensitive-field policy: do not blanket-redact ordinary configuration, paths or version information, and never reveal protected values merely because verbose output is enabled.

For every new or changed public command: Identify its output pattern and reuse presentation result primitives plus the invocation-owned logging/linear view. Search existing renderers first; extend the shared owner when behavior is missing instead of building a local spinner, logger, color palette or table formatter. Exercise the real compiled entry point. Check startup feedback, one successful outcome and an applicable failure, including meaningful terminal step closure. A renderer unit test alone does not prove the command selected that renderer. Check ordinary human output, redirected/no-color output, JSON stdout/stderr separation and quiet behavior. Use focused rendering checks for narrow/long layouts and concurrent output when relevant; use a capable terminal for changed redraw behavior. State unavailable terminal/platform qualification explicitly. Confirm the payload exceptions, exit codes, sensitive-field handling and help/version fast path remain intact. Presentation must not change tool flags, plans, cache identity, evidence or policy. Update the owning reference and record actual verification. Fix inconsistencies in the changed command; record unrelated command-family gaps rather than claiming repository-wide compliance or launching an unbounded visual rewrite.

oyzu --help, oyzu help build, nested --help, --version and unknown-command diagnostics use the built-in command catalog. They work with an empty PATH, malformed project files and a nonexistent -C directory. They do not load project configuration, refresh enterprise policy, open tool stores, initialize backend workers or contact services. No installation or platform account is required. The operating system still loads the binary and Oyzu checks its executable identity to distinguish native tool shims. Actual run list/discover inspect a project; which validates the frozen tool selection. Those are explicit operations, not static command help, and retain their configuration and verification requirements. A native tool shim's help continues to invoke that selected tool. The public CLI and reusable application command layer share execution behavior; see the architecture boundary. Local run tasks retain stdin. In text mode, tasks recording a bundle tee full stdout/stderr to the caller and dist/logs, including in quiet mode, without replaying output at completion. Their output descriptors are pipes. Tasks marked interactive = true instead inherit terminal stdout/stderr; those streams cannot also be captured, so their bundle stdout/stderr files are empty. Non-bundled tasks also inherit output directly. JSON captures task output and keeps stdout as the final result. See task streams.

JSON stdout contains one result without Oyzu-added headings, ANSI styling or progress. Existing structured result shapes are retained where available. Oyzu diagnostics on stderr use JSON Lines, including non-build warnings. Read stdout for the command result. Native pass-through streams retain their documented behavior. Setup, operation and argument-parsing errors contain error and exitCode, with a nonzero process exit. JSON help/version return their text in output with exitCode: 0. exec --json captures child output in stdout and stderr strings and returns exitCode, also preserving that exit code in Oyzu. Input remains inherited; captured output appears when the child exits, not as a live terminal. The result's capture object discloses inherited stdin, piped stdout/stderr, no output TTY, non-streaming delivery and lossy UTF-8 decoding; invocationId correlates diagnostics. Non-UTF-8 bytes use replacement characters. JSON run outcome records disclose file-based stdout/stderr capture, inherited stdin, non-TTY/non-streaming output, lossy decoding and invocation correlation. Default execution remains pass-through.

activate, deactivate, environment hooks and env --shell SHELL emit executable shell code by default: headings would break evaluation. With --json, they return { "shell": "…", "script": "…" }. Evaluate raw code, never the JSON envelope. JSON mode retains the same activation/session-record effects. env inspection stays redacted; explicitly requested shell payloads contain actual assignments in both modes.

install SPEC, update and uninstall lead with the outcome (✓ Installed go 1.26.8), then indented facts: what was declared and where, the lock and its platforms, replaced requirements and notes about other scopes. --dry-run starts with Dry run · no files were changed. The inspection commands use an outcome line, an aligned table and an Attention section for unresolved rows; statuses are words (ok, not installed, blocked, deprecated, stale lock, ambiguous), never colour alone. All of them support --json. See tool commands.

tools resolve and tools evidence (see reference) use the inspection pattern: a title, an outcome line (✓ complete, ! attention), the snapshot, an aligned table of records (status words, never colour alone), then Unsupported platforms, Errors, Needs attention and Next steps sections. --json prints exactly one artifact-set document on stdout (the diagnostic lines of evidence, such as EVIDENCE_FETCH, go to stderr). Exit 3 means a complete document with undecided or unverified items. Recipe-supplied text is control-character escaped. Verified by the compiled-CLI tests in tests/integration/recipe_resolve.rs (human no-colour text, both JSON exit codes and error envelopes) and the proof runner; narrow-terminal wrapping reuses the shared table and was observed at 80 columns only.

oyzu discover answers "what does Oyzu see here?". It prints one block per target (the name oyzu build <target> accepts): builder, whether build.yaml or detection from native files chose it, package manager, version, location relative to the project root, which tasks are part of builds and which are development-only (with the reason when one is unavailable). It reads configuration and native files without running project code. The task catalogue and commands belong to oyzu run list; --json returns the complete discovery record. With no targets it explains what to add or where to run. See build tasks.

oyzu tools list groups installations by tool (rust (core) · 12 installations · 17.0 GB), each with a Version / Platform / Size / Used by / ID table. ID is the start of the installation digest: it tells apart installs of one version that differ by recipe or platform ABI. --details adds location, tool identity and the full installation digest per row. The lead line totals installations, tools, unreferenced installs and disk use.

A bundle is the directory oyzu build writes (dist/ by default) or an exported OCI archive. oyzu inspect with no argument verifies the current project's dist/; a project root is accepted for its dist/. A missing bundle names where Oyzu looked and suggests oyzu build. On success the human view leads with ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded|failed, then the run and source identity and tables of targets (builder, platform), actions (status, exit, gate), artifacts (path, size, platform, short digest), reports and diagnostics. It states that verification checks recorded digests, not who produced the build. An OCI archive shows kind, platforms, size and digests. --json keeps the full manifest. See build bundles.

oyzu.toml settings (including tools.* pins) inherit from the Git worktree root, while build.yaml does not inherit: the nearest ancestor build.yaml selects the build. A project nested in a repository therefore sees the repository's tool pins. Pass --root . to fix both roots at the current directory and stop inheritance (see configuration).

Human failures from a command print ✗ <what failed and how to recover> with the diagnostic code underneath (for example COMMAND_FAILED), not a raw [Error] [oyzu::commands] envelope. A message that already leads with its own stable code (✗ CONFIG_SYNTAX: …, ✗ REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED: …) omits the generic code underneath; --json keeps its {"error", "exitCode"} object and -q keeps the plain error line. Internal pipeline scopes are shown as words (Setup, Preflight, Source, Plan); generated platform target ids are shown as target · os/arch. Running a task prints a heading, shared lifecycle rows and the task result, followed by the native tool output unchanged.

Diagnostic prose redacts only the credential-bearing part: a URL with userinfo becomes [sensitive diagnostic detail withheld], URL queries and fragments become ?[redacted], key=value / key: value forms for credential names keep the name and replace the value, and Authorization: or Bearer redact the rest of the line. Ordinary URLs and prose stay readable. Configuration display still hides any value that looks credential-bearing. Native child output is not rewritten.

Scripts parsing formerly JSON-only pin, discovery, bundle/tool inspection or configuration output must now pass --json. Human formatting is not a parsing contract. Result schemas remain command-specific; this does not change build evidence or introduce a universal result schema. CLI tests cover human defaults, both flag positions, structured errors, help/version, child execution and shell payloads. Measured results and outstanding checks are in implementation status. Windows verification does not qualify other hosts.

Global -v/--verbose enables debug, -vv enables trace, -q/--quiet selects warn, and --log-level error|warn|info|debug|trace selects an explicit threshold. Default is info. Options work on either side of a subcommand; arguments after -- belong to the child. More than two -v or one -q, or combining these controls, is an argument error before project loading. One explicit CLI control overrides all of OYZU_LOG. Otherwise this optional UTF-8 environment value accepts a level or comma-separated target=level directives, optionally preceded by a default level (info when omitted): $env:OYZU_LOG = 'warn,oyzu::executor=trace' oyzu run foo oyzu run foo --json -v Remove-Item Env:OYZU_LOG Targets are oyzu::commands, oyzu::config, oyzu::discovery, oyzu::tools, oyzu::acquisition, oyzu::executor, oyzu::builders and oyzu::reports. An exact target directive overrides the default. Unknown or duplicate targets, empty directives and invalid levels fail. Overridden environment filters are not read. Help/version ignore OYZU_LOG, including invalid values. These are invocation presentation options, not oyzu.toml settings. RUST_LOG does not control Oyzu diagnostics or enable dependency payload logging. Quiet hides routine Oyzu progress and the interactive dashboard. It preserves command results, warnings, errors and native child output. Verbosity does not change native flags/environment, plans, cache inputs, report gates or production eligibility. Logging is local, offline-capable and needs no account, service or new persistent sink. Human diagnostics identify severity and the affected work. Operational failures also identify the running executable/version, selected directory, host platform and observation identity when available. Help/version/syntax remain independent of runtime initialization. JSON diagnostic envelopes retain the existing event fields and add severity, target, invocationId, operationId and parentOperationId. Diagnostic events contain type, code and message, with numeric duration_ms for completed operations. Retained build journals now carry the same correlation fields and observed warning/error diagnostics, independently of console detail filtering. Filtered console projections may have sequence gaps. Sequence orders observations within an invocation; it does not establish causal ordering between native processes. Consumers must tolerate additive fields and event kinds. The existing unreleased manifest/envelope schemas gain optional invocationId in place; actions can carry namespaced log references and the explicit not-started outcome for interruption before launch. Reuse can identify the serving cache tier (local or remote), independently of its producer. All thresholds use the same field admission. No environment/header maps or unrestricted argument arrays are logged. Command events withhold arguments; credential-bearing parts of diagnostic prose are redacted (see Redaction). Arbitrary child output and explicitly requested shell payloads are not rewritten and may contain secrets. Trace is not an HTTP dump or a secret-inspection mode. Pin's human output includes a deduplicated execution-platform coverage section. It describes resolved metadata, not installed availability or platform execution qualification. JSON retains the full platform-specific compiler_metadata recipes.

Outside a project, oyzu run lists nearby projects by relative directory rather than importing their tasks under generated identifiers. The navigation lookup searches at most three directory levels, skips hidden/generated directories, stops below a project boundary and returns at most 32 projects. It reads no child configuration or native metadata and runs no tools. Change into a listed project or use oyzu -C <project> run. JSON returns status: "outside-project", directory, projects, searchDepth, limit and nextStep. An empty lookup fails with PROJECT_NOT_FOUND and the searched directory; requesting a task from the parent fails with TASK_PROJECT_REQUIRED before loading a child project. Explicit workspace roots remain workspaces and use the ordinary task listing. An unknown task returns TASK_NOT_FOUND, the selected project directory, available task names and a close spelling suggestion when one exists. It also points to oyzu run and oyzu -C <project> run <task> for recovery. No task-running preamble appears for this failure. Native execution is announced only after task selection and preparation; completed task rows include the exit code and duration, for example Failed (exit 7 after 0.20s). The process preserves the failed child's exit code; task JSON records retain exit_code and add duration_ms (execution time excluding discovery and tool preparation). oyzu run list opens with a count (Available tasks · 8 across 1 target), then shows one table: the Task / Source / Command header appears once and every group shares its column widths. Tasks are grouped by target (for example cli and docs), with ungrouped user tasks under Project; each group heading shows its builder and task count. Listing is a quick lookup, so it prints no progress or logger lines. Each row shows the qualified runnable name, source and effective command arguments. Builder-discovered tasks are labeled Inferred with their provider; TOML-defined tasks show the effective source file, relative to the project when possible. (override) indicates a replacement of an inferred task or an earlier configuration definition. Native package scripts discovered through a builder are also labeled inferred; this distinguishes discovery from an Oyzu TOML definition, not script authorship. Cyan headings separate groups, inferred sources are muted and authored sources are purple. ui.color, NO_COLOR and terminal detection control color; Explicit ui.color=always/never wins; in auto mode NO_COLOR disables color and CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 enables it when NO_COLOR is absent. Long rows use lossless labeled records on narrow terminals. Unavailable tasks retain their reason. Commands quote arguments descriptively; they are not a portable shell script. Dependencies and hooks may add execution beyond that row. Credential-like command previews are withheld and terminal controls escaped. Do not embed credentials in task command arguments; use the supported environment or secret mechanisms instead. Listing reads discovery and resolved configuration but executes no tasks or native tools. JSON retains the task map and adds each task's origin object: kind (inferred or user-defined), source (full configuration source or null) and override (boolean). Existing argv and redacted environment fields retain their contracts. No configuration or lock files are changed by listing.
CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/configuration.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them.

publish.default selects a named OCI destination or publication set when oyzu publish has no --destination. publish.destinations is a typed map of names to registry, repository, and optional paired usernameEnv/passwordEnv credential references. publish.sets maps names to nonempty destination lists. Destination and set names must be distinct. Every selected destination is required. publish.requirements contains provenance (bundlePath, accepted Ed25519 publicKey, builderId) and signing (keyEnv, publicKey). Public keys are base64 raw 32-byte keys; keyEnv references a separately provisioned base64 32-byte signing seed. Never store secret values in project configuration. Evidence paths resolve relative to the source declaring effective requirements. These settings use the ordinary cascade, selected profiles and mandatory constraints. Each destinations map, sets map, and requirements object is atomic: a later source replaces the whole value instead of merging nested entries. The settings govern standalone safeguards; they cannot grant managed publication authority. See publishing for the complete example, evidence profile, digest-only coordinates and current limits. The configuration engine implements the public OEP-0002 draft in Rust. Its CLI and wire formats remain experimental; implementation authorization does not change the proposal's maintainer-review status. See the acceptance contract and measured implementation status. oyzu config show presents resolved status and profile first, followed by setting tables grouped by namespace and the computation digest. Keys retain their exact spelling; booleans use true/false and empty lists use []. Environment values and task bodies remain redacted under configuration inspection's contract; use oyzu env for environment inspection. --json retains the structured result. See the CLI style guide.

Oyzu captures caller environment hints once when opening the configuration session, before build workers set their own CI=true. Detection is offline and independent of terminals, hostnames, network access and operating system. This is unverified execution context, never runner authentication, authorization or release eligibility. The following nonempty markers identify providers. Empty values and the trimmed, case-insensitive values false, 0, no, and off disable that individual marker. Provider Marker GitHub Actions / Gitea Actions GITHUB_ACTIONS / GITEA_ACTIONS GitLab / Azure Pipelines GITLAB_CI / TF_BUILD Jenkins / TeamCity / Bamboo JENKINS_URL / TEAMCITY_VERSION / bamboo_planKey Buildkite / CircleCI / Travis / AppVeyor BUILDKITE / CIRCLECI / TRAVIS / APPVEYOR Bitbucket Pipelines / Bitrise BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER / BITRISE_IO Google Cloud Build BUILDER_OUTPUT AWS CodeBuild / Harness CODEBUILD_BUILD_ARN / HARNESS_BUILD_ID Codefresh / GoCD / Prow CF_BUILD_ID / GO_PIPELINE_LABEL / PROW_JOB_ID Drone / Cirrus / Semaphore DRONE / CIRRUS_CI / SEMAPHORE Netlify / Vercel / Xcode Cloud NETLIFY / VERCEL / CI_XCODE_PROJECT TaskCluster requires both TASK_ID and RUN_ID to be nonempty (RUN_ID=0 is valid). Additionally, exact CI=woodpecker, CI_NAME=sourcehut, and CI_NAME=codeship identify those providers. Any enabled CI value selects CI behavior even when the provider is unknown. Multiple provider matches are retained in sorted order; CI=false disables only the generic hint, not an enabled vendor marker. With no matching signal the context is local. Unknown platforms without a recognized marker must supply the conventional CI=true; no detector can identify every future or privately hosted system without a signal. Generic variables such as BUILD_ID alone are deliberately insufficient. config explain exposes executionContext with ci, sorted providers, and matched variable names in signals. Values and private runner URLs are not recorded. Build plans retain the same context in oyzu.dev/execution-context. The detector follows the environment-marker approach used by ci-info; its implementation is first-party and adds no dependency or copied vendor dataset. Plain oyzu build defaults to artifact building and packaging locally. In CI it also admits the builder's available test, lint and format-check stages. Existing checks.required, a positive coverage minimum, and explicit task prerequisites remain effective locally. oyzu build --full enables all available quality gates regardless of context; it does not change context detection or profile selection. config explain includes the resolved fullBuild request (default false); build plans record fullRequested. The existing oyzu --profile ci build also requests full stages but selects the CI profile. CI needs no extra flags. A different profile or --no-profile does not turn off detected CI checks. See build context behavior.

plugins.development maps a built-in builder id such as go/app to an absolute plugin executable path. It is accepted only from user, machine or administrative configuration and replaces that builder's native host operations for the invocation. See local development plugin bindings. plugins.packages maps such an id to { archive, sha256 }: a verified, installed package whose selection oyzu.lock pins. Same scopes. See plugin packages.

Project trust controls are trust.enabled (boolean, default true) and trust.parents (absolute folder paths, default []). They and platform.url, platform.account, cache.remote, cache.ciRemote are rejected in project/local scope, including profile overlays. Set them in user/global, machine or administrative configuration. Supported invocation environment sources are OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST, OYZU_PLATFORM_URL, OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT, OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE and OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE; each overrides ordinary files while remaining subject to administrative constraints. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST accepts true/false, on/off, yes/no or 1/0. See folder trust for the environment application boundary and native user-state records.

build.yaml now accepts a builds mapping with uses, path, platforms, depends_on, materialize, bindings and with per entry. depends_on is an ordering-only list of producer build names; it does not transfer artifacts. bindings remains discovery-only and fails captured-build admission. Configuration owns normalization and freezes all declared platforms; builders own validation of with. See the Rust build options for the implemented options and execution limits. This is a partial implementation of the proposed build model, not support for every future example. Tool requirements remain in TOML and lock identities remain in oyzu.lock. The previous flat inventory is retained for compatibility; do not mix it with a builds envelope.

Configuration commands default to human-readable output. Pass global --json for structured results and errors; see CLI output. Use an Oyzu CLI built from this branch; these commands are not a promise about older releases. Standalone configuration inspection and editing require no platform account, Docker, native ecosystem toolchain or network service. The client has Windows, macOS and Linux implementations; platform qualification and measured checks are tracked in implementation status. Running tasks or builds additionally requires their explicitly provisioned native tools. In an otherwise empty directory named config-demo, save this as oyzu.toml: [build] jobs = 2 [profile] default = "dev" [profiles.dev.build] jobs = 3 [ui] color = "never" Run these commands from its parent directory. Expected values assume standalone operation with no administrative constraints, local overrides or OYZU_PROFILE selection: oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --no-profile config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config set build.jobs 4 --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config unset build.jobs --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs The successive get results are 3, 2, 4, and 2. Validation reports success; with --json it returns valid: true. Removing the profile assignment exposes the base value; it does not restore the old value of 3. Set/unset return the destination path and updated key. No project task runs in this walkthrough.

oyzu --root path/to/project config show --json oyzu --root path/to/project config explain build.jobs --json oyzu --root path/to/project config profiles oyzu --root path/to/project config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root path/to/project --profile integration run test oyzu --root path/to/project --no-profile run test --root explicitly fixes both build and configuration roots. Otherwise the nearest ancestor build.yaml within the current Git worktree selects the build; configuration still inherits from the Git worktree root. Outside Git, the outermost ancestor with Oyzu configuration or a build declaration bounds inheritance, falling back to the invocation directory. With no build declaration, that boundary remains the conventional-discovery root. -C / --directory selects the invocation directory; --root alone also selects that directory. Git boundaries require recognizable repository metadata: HEAD plus the common objects and refs directories. A .git file must contain a gitdir: <path> pointer to that metadata; linked worktrees use its commondir pointer for the common directories. Relative pointers are resolved from their declaring directory. An unborn repository and packed refs remain valid boundaries; no commit or loose branch ref is required. Empty .git directories, malformed pointers and missing metadata do not define a workspace. They are left intact. Recognition reads bounded local metadata without running Git, executing configuration or establishing repository integrity. Conservative nested repository/submodule exclusions during target traversal remain in effect. Entering an independent nested example and running oyzu build --plan therefore selects the example without --root. Its oyzu.lock and build outputs belong to that selected root. Parent inventories are not merged, and automatic discovery skips nested build roots. An explicit parent target path remains authoritative. Configuration retains normal project/local precedence, relative paths retain their declaring-file origin, and machine/enterprise constraints remain enforced. A selected build root may declare its default profile; ordinary target subdirectories cannot. Explicit composition and shared-workspace lock ownership are not implemented. Relative task cwd values are now relative to the TOML file that declares them. For a root-file override of api:test, use cwd = "api/checks" to select that directory. Multiple targets cannot own the same native build unit; use distinct project paths or distinct builders where appropriate. Sources resolve in this order: built-ins, verified corporate defaults, protected local administrative defaults, machine configuration, user configuration, root-to-target oyzu.toml, eligible root-to-target oyzu.local.toml, and invocation compatibility inputs. Each source applies its base followed by the selected profile. Siblings receive separate snapshots. Arrays replace, tasks replace atomically, and [overrides].remove removes explicit environment/task entries. Environment removals also unset inherited variables during development task execution. A task environment can replace a global variable with the same spelling, but case aliases such as TOKEN and token are rejected across the combined environment on every host. Known tool aliases share that same precedence. For example, project node = "22" overrides global "oyzu:node" = "latest"; a selected profile can override its base through either spelling. Inspection retains the spellings with their effective value and winning provenance. Lock ownership follows the winning source. Declaring multiple aliases for one tool in the same overlay remains ambiguous. Administrative constraints bind the selected value regardless of its spelling. Profile selection uses explicit --profile or --no-profile, inherited task selection, OYZU_PROFILE, the eligible root/default selector, inferred CI's empty ci profile, then no profile. Names grant no authority. Inferred CI excludes user computation settings and local files; --local-overrides requests local files, subject to administrative restrictions. Excluded local files are not parsed. config show, get, explain, profiles, and validate do not execute project tasks. If resolution is blocked, show and explain return an explicit unresolved status without effective values; validate remains the failing validation command. The credential-origin and trust-control scope ban is an exception: platform.url, platform.account, cache.remote, cache.ciRemote, trust.enabled and trust.parents in project/local sources are hard errors even for show and explain, in human and JSON output and in CI when that source is included. The error names the key, source and user/global or administrative remedy. Configuration inspection displays ordinary environment settings and path arrays; credential-like environment names and recognizable sensitive values remain redacted, as do task bodies. Discovery/task listing also redacts environment values. Explain includes source histories, byte spans, exclusions, constraint source IDs and the effective computation digest. Warnings carry severity, source byte spans when available, target scope, and a remedy without including the configured value. Unknown optional settings warn and stay inert; known invalid values, unsupported required capabilities, duplicate keys and unsupported schema majors fail. --strict rejects optional warnings. --all-profiles validates inactive capability requirements and profile outcomes.

oyzu --root path/to/project config set build.jobs 8 --project oyzu --root path/to/project config set checks.required '["tests"]' --json-value --local oyzu --root path/to/project --profile dev config set ui.color never --global oyzu --root path/to/project config unset build.jobs --project Exactly one of --global (the user configuration file), --project, or --local is required. --directory can select a contained nested project scope. unset removes an assignment in that file and exposes inherited values; it does not create a removal tombstone. Ordinary edits remain available to repair invalid values even when resolution is blocked; they do not activate values or alter protected records. Edits preserve unrelated comments and unknown syntax, validate known types/scopes, and compare the original bytes before atomic replacement. Concurrent changes produce CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT. A small .oyzu-config-edit.lock coordinates Oyzu writers and is excluded from source snapshots. Only an explicit --profile NAME directs an edit into that profile. An inferred/default profile does not change the write destination: an edit without --profile writes the base section. Scalar booleans and numbers are parsed by type; strings are literal. Use --json-value for arrays or objects. The array example above uses shell quoting supported by PowerShell and POSIX shells. Edits cannot repair malformed TOML syntax; correct that syntax in an editor first. They cannot modify administrative or enrollment records.

All config commands default to human-readable output. Add global --json for structured results and errors. The JSON schema is experimental. Command Result and important behavior show Effective values, selected profile, digest, diagnostics and resolution status get KEY One effective value (a JSON value with --json); fails if the key has no effective value explain [KEY] Resolution evidence, optionally narrowed to a key; includes origins and constraints profiles Available profiles, selected profile and selection reason validate [--strict] [--all-profiles] valid: true on success; nonzero exit on validation failure status Standalone/enrolled state and managed cache health; does not refresh over the network refresh Explicit online policy acquisition; returns revision and offline deadline; requires protected enrollment set / unset Changes one ordinary file and reports its destination; does not establish that the edited value is effective show, get and explain accept mutually exclusive --global, --project and --local flags. These inspect only the selected file: the user configuration, oyzu.toml in the selected directory, or oyzu.local.toml there, respectively. For example, oyzu config get build.jobs --global reads the user declaration; oyzu -C packages/api config show --project shows that directory's declarations. Without a scope flag, the merged effective configuration remains the default. Scoped reads do not inject defaults, inspect other sources, contact policy services or execute tasks. They preserve the normal inspection redaction. An explicit --profile NAME overlays only that profile from the selected file; automatic/default profile selection does not apply to file inspection. show/explain report the source, scope and whether the file exists, with empty values when absent; get fails when the key is not declared there. These are declarations, not a claim that execution policy allows the requested values. TOML syntax failures identify file:line:column (one-based Unicode character coordinates) and the parser's reason, including during set/unset. Source snippets are omitted to keep configuration values out of diagnostics. Correct malformed syntax in an editor before retrying. Strict validation retains every warning's key, source, available line/column and byte span, message and remedy; human errors list them and JSON errors include a diagnostics array. Strict validation still fails instead of silently accepting the warnings. Human explain groups exact setting keys with effective values and their last source. Multiple origins appear as an ordered resolution history; the last source does not imply it supplied every element of a merged value. Only nonempty policy restrictions, exclusions and diagnostics are expanded. With no restrictions it prints one policy summary rather than an empty entry for every setting. Source paths omit Windows extended-path prefixes for display. Ordinary environment paths and compiler settings remain visible. Sensitive values stay redacted. explain <key> narrows the view; --json retains the complete metadata, including byte spans, constraint source IDs, context signals and digest. show and explain can exit successfully with status: "unresolved" and no effective values. status can likewise return an unhealthy managed state successfully. Automation must inspect these fields or use validate as its configuration gate. Execution errors are reported on stderr with a nonzero exit status. Inspection does not run tasks, but resolving an enrolled configuration can contact the policy endpoint and update its cache. Thus inspection is not necessarily network-free or free of persistent state changes.
