Not part of any action key tools.<name> Nonempty string; absent Explicit requests fail execution until a verified installation binding exists; no tool installation is performed env.<name> Literal string or { secret = "reference" }; absent Literal environment overlay; secret references require a future authorized consumer tasks.<name> Task record; absent Atomic task replacement; see syntax below docker.apparmorProfile Profile name; host-derived oyzu-buildkit when the detected Linux user-namespace restriction requires it, otherwise unconfined docker.frontends List of image references pinned by digest; empty # syntax= frontends a Dockerfile may request. A request matches an entry with the same repository and the same digest, or the same tag when the request has no digest. Oyzu's BuildKit frontend runs the approved frontend; any other request fails with FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED naming the requested and approved references. See Docker frontends Environment names use ASCII letters, digits and underscores, beginning with a letter or underscore; the OYZU_ prefix is reserved case-insensitively. Values are not expressions or interpolation programs. Inspection redaction does not make literal environment values a secret store: literals can participate in build inputs/evidence. Do not use a literal as a substitute for the deferred secret consumer. Task records select either run (a shell command) or argv (an argument array), and accept shell, cwd, env, depends_on, inputs, outputs, cache, interactive and reports. cache = true with outputs makes an authored task cacheable by oyzu build (its inputs may only add paths inside its target); outputs on a hook lets the cache follow it; see authored tasks. Local oyzu run inherits stdin. Text-mode tasks recording a bundle tee stdout/stderr live and retain them in dist/logs; interactive = true instead preserves real output terminal descriptors, with no captured stdout/stderr logs. Tasks without a bundle inherit output directly. For PowerShell run scripts, interactive = true also omits -NonInteractive; it does not make captured builds interactive. JSON mode captures output while retaining stdin; see task streams and limits. Task env contains strings. Task execution also requires a discoverable native project. For example, with Node explicitly provisioned and a package.json containing {"name":"config-demo","version":"1.0.0"}, add this to oyzu.toml: [tasks.hello] argv = ["node", "-e", "console.log('hello')"] oyzu --root path/to/project run hello executes that command. A higher-priority task record replaces the entire record rather than merging its fields. To remove inherited environment/task entries, use dotted key strings in a removal list: Additional arguments after -- are appended to an argv task, including an argv that already contains -c or -Command (for example a Python expression). Tasks authored with run reject additional arguments; choose argv when a task needs parameters. This distinction follows the declared task form, not the spelling of arguments passed to the native executable. [overrides] remove = ["env.DEMO_MODE", "tasks.hello"] The following keys are administrative-only and cannot appear in ordinary files or profiles: Key Type and default Meaning config.localOverridesInCi Boolean; false Whether the local override request is eligible in CI config.allowedProfiles Set of names, including @none; absent Restricts selection when supplied tools.allowed Set of canonical tool IDs; absent Restricts tool eligibility tools.ignore Set of tool names; absent Folder-scoped: silences best-effort tool detection of the named tools (managed tools, host programs, fetching packages) for targets in that folder and below. Never removes a primary toolchain; an explicit [tools] pin still provides the tool. Ignored detections show in -v and --json as ignored by tools.ignore in <path> tools.catalogs Ordered string array; ["public"] Catalog preference; unavailable protected bindings block execution registries.routes Route array; [] Each entry has protocol, scope, connectorId; protocols are npm, pypi, maven, cargo, go, oci, tools; standalone Node/Go installation supports explicit host tool bindings; real Node proxy acceptance passed, Go proxy acceptance remains pending; other connector execution remains deferred npm.sources Set of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in /; [] Extra locations an isolated npm build may download locked packages from, in addition to https://registry.npmjs.org/. For example, https://codeload.github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tar.gz/ admits a package that pins a public GitHub commit as a tarball. Declare it in package.json as that same HTTPS tarball URL and record the URL and its sha512 in the lockfile; a git+https or github: spec in package.json is refused, because native npm would refetch it as a git dependency instead of using the captured tarball. Each package still needs the lockfile's sha512 integrity, which is verified. Credentials, queries and fragments are refused. Applies to the npm builder only; git+https lock entries remain unsupported fetches.sources Set of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in /; absent Administrative allowlist for declared fetches. Absent, any HTTPS URL is admitted. Set, each fetch URL and every redirect must fall under a listed prefix, or the build fails with SOURCE_DENIED or REDIRECT_DENIED; an empty list admits none. Project configuration cannot set it. Credentials, queries and fragments are refused maven.snapshotRepositories Set of HTTPS repository base URLs ending in /; [] (off) Snapshot repositories that captured Maven acquisition may use for snapshot version paths only, each through its own broker source; every other path keeps the Maven Central or session-approved route. Credentials, queries, fragments and plain HTTP are refused. Snapshot inputs are inventoried in the dependency snapshot, and a build whose version intent is not a development snapshot fails rather than use one. See Maven snapshot repositories

Host Machine directory User configuration User state directory Windows ProgramData known folder + Oyzu RoamingAppData known folder + Oyzu/config.toml LocalAppData known folder + Oyzu/state macOS /Library/Application Support/Oyzu ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/state Linux /etc/oyzu $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/oyzu/config.toml, fallback ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml $XDG_STATE_HOME/oyzu, fallback ~/.local/state/oyzu Windows paths come from native known-folder APIs. Relative XDG paths warn and use the home fallback. The machine directory contains ordinary config.toml, protected admin-settings.json, and protected enrollment management.json. Project/local files are named oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml; keep personal local overrides out of version control. Oyzu does not auto-enroll the machine. For persistent user data, including the tool store, an absolute Windows HOME that differs from the native profile selects <HOME>/AppData/Local/Oyzu. This lets disposable homes isolate tool caches and rollback records. With HOME unset or naming the normal profile, native LocalAppData redirection is preserved. A relative HOME fails with CONFIG_SCOPE; use an absolute path or unset it. This data override does not redirect the configuration and managed policy state locations in the table, or the separate action/image cache locations. Existing data is not moved or deleted when selecting another home. OYZU_USER_CONFIG optionally selects an absolute user configuration file, useful for disposable environments and testing user defaults without modifying a real profile. Relative paths are rejected. The file retains user-level precedence and authority; this setting cannot redirect machine policy, enrollment or state. Its sibling oyzu.lock owns user-default tool pins. Unset the variable to return to the native user configuration location. Help/version do not read this setting. Managed state includes signed policy entries under the user state directory and integrity pointers/high-water state in the native credential store. Ordinary configuration edits do not change that state. Source capture enforces size/complexity budgets, including a 1 MiB file limit, and detects concurrent source changes rather than mixing revisions. This configuration format has no include mechanism or executable configuration language.

Native locations follow OEP-0002: Windows known folders, macOS Application Support, and Linux /etc/oyzu plus absolute XDG user locations. Protected files require administrative ownership and permissions. Windows uses native ACL/handle checks; Unix checks root ownership and write permissions; macOS also examines extended ACL entries on the opened object and rejects non-root mutation grants using the native descriptor ACL API. An insecure, unreadable or malformed enrollment never becomes standalone mode. admin-settings.json uses the same typed constraint evaluator as corporate policy. Locks, allowed whole values, numeric bounds and required sets intersect independently of ordinary precedence. Required checks cannot be removed by empty ordinary arrays. The build planner requires configured checks to have actual actions/report contracts; report collection enforces the coverage minimum, including missing/zero-denominator failures. config status reports enrollment and cached-policy status. config refresh performs a headless request to the enrolled platform's public configuration-context endpoint. Signed responses use pinned Ed25519 keys, canonical JSON, identity/context binding, monotonic sequences, expiry and explicit offline permissions. Cache entries are content-addressed and flushed before an OS credential-store pointer commits them. A corrupt entry can only be repaired from a newly verified online response. Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain and Linux Secret Service hold integrity state. If that service is unavailable, managed execution fails; standalone use does not need it. Transport backoff never extends signed deadlines. Server denial cannot become offline permission.

Rust targets can declare a finite rust object with optional features and a targets list of Cargo triples. Tool requirements remain in TOML and resolved identities in oyzu.lock; the YAML object rejects toolchain pins. It produces explicit native binary task definitions, described in Rust binary targets, including the unfinished locked-tool execution handoff. It cannot be combined with captured platform matrices. Isolated builds reject that native-only intent instead of dropping its requirements. build.yaml describes target intent separately from the TOML cascade. Its optional application container field is a boolean or a finite object with base, user, workdir and entrypoint; see Python application containers for types, defaults and current runtime support. Capture validates and freezes that object with the target inventory. config validate rejects malformed option values without resolving images or executing a build. The object introduces no task language or additional precedence layer. Administrative execution checks and resolved owner settings still apply to generated image actions.

The Docker adapter registers docker.apparmorProfile. It replaces direct adapter reads of OYZU_BUILDKIT_APPARMOR_PROFILE; the legacy environment variable remains a diagnosed invocation input and faces the same policy constraints. The default still detects the host's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. Builder namespaces stay behind the crate-private Builder contract. A frozen build configuration contributes its digest to target/action records. Formatting, profile names and presentation preferences do not affect that configuration digest. Policy revision and online/offline context remain separate evidence. No policy snapshot grants signing, publishing or credential issuance. Build preparation and planning require the resolved invocation snapshot and every selected target's snapshot, including inferred targets without configuration files. Missing internal snapshots fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE; they never disable policy checks or cause adapters to recalculate defaults. Library callers must use discovery to obtain this state; serialized discovery JSON is an inspection result, not a resumable workspace. Rediscover the workspace if that state is missing. Docker reads its execution profile from the admitted snapshot before preparation starts. Later edits to live configuration files do not change an already frozen plan; start a new invocation to resolve them. The current native tool-store, authenticated platform-session, connector-binding and shell-secret-consumer implementations are not completed by this configuration change; the remote action cache is an experimental development-scope implementation that signs in only with a token from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or a CI job's ID tokens (see the action cache). Explicit tool requests that cannot be bound to a verified installation are rejected before builds. Enforced routes/catalogs requiring unavailable bindings fail before public acquisition. Managed builders that still require public dependency preparation are blocked; offline-capable local Docker and Helm preparation remains separate from those network paths. Development secret references require an authorized consumer and are not substituted into build literals. build.jobs bounds concurrent ready actions. The invocation uses the smallest admitted root/target ceiling; each target retains serial mutation and hook order. Targets have private workspaces and output roots. Dependency or deferred-report failure blocks consumers while independent targets can finish. ui.color controls human-readable task labels and outcome statuses: always emits ANSI color, never disables it, and auto enables it only when the relevant output stream is a terminal. Task-specific resolved preferences apply to that task; root tasks use root preferences. JSON output remains unstyled. Cache preferences do not grant cache credentials or trust: a remote hit is a development result. These boundaries are deliberate failures rather than claims that all OEP-0002 ecosystem and platform integration acceptance cases pass. Three-host ACL/keychain qualification, signed server interoperability, authenticated logout/account-switch flows, complete connector routing and tool-store integration remain release gates. Development execution checks tool eligibility, explicit tool requests and protected routing/catalog requirements before any prerequisite or hook runs. Managed host tasks remain blocked until approved development execution and connector bindings exist; the host runner cannot claim to enforce managed network routing. Task-specific and native-adapter environment additions must satisfy administrative environment restrictions. In a single-target nested project, the target's final task cascade determines whether a root operation is replaced or removed, consistently with inspection and build planning.

Diagnostic or symptom Recovery CONFIG_SYNTAX, duplicate keys Correct the source file's syntax/duplicate declaration, then validate CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, CONFIG_SCOPE Use the registered type and permitted scope; ordinary set/unset can repair invalid values CONFIG_PROFILE_UNKNOWN Inspect profile declarations and select an existing name; use --no-profile only if policy permits Optional-setting warning / strict failure Correct the spelling or remove inert optional settings; ordinary validation does not execute unknown syntax Unsupported schema major or required capability Use a compatible client; do not remove a requirement unless the project no longer needs it CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT, CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED Reconcile conflicting administrative constraints or choose an allowed value; unavailable execution bindings require their implementation/provisioning CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT Re-read the file and retry the intended edit; do not overwrite another writer's changes CONFIG_LIMIT Reduce file size, nesting or configuration entries, including inactive profile data POLICY_INVALID Inspect enrollment protection and policy/cache validity; an administrator may need to repair bootstrap permissions or signing configuration POLICY_EXPIRED, POLICY_UNAVAILABLE Restore endpoint/native credential-store availability and run config refresh; failure never converts an enrolled machine to standalone POLICY_CLOCK_UNCERTAIN Correct clock problems and reconcile online; do not erase rollback-protection state to bypass the error Offline execution requires explicit signed permission and remains bounded by both signed expiry and maximum offline age (at most 24 hours). CI requires online policy. Transport retry/backoff preserves these deadlines; denial and malformed responses do not authorize offline fallback. Explicit refresh can fail while an older valid cache remains stored. A corrupt cache entry requires a newly verified online response; damaged integrity-store state can require administrator intervention. Refresh rechecks time after I/O, so a request that finishes after a deadline does not extend authorization. Changing protected bootstrap pins invalidates the previous cache binding. Recovery requires an online response verified against the current pins with a strictly newer policy sequence; existing high-water state remains in force. Do not delete credential-store state as a key-rotation procedure. Cache commit ordering preserves the old committed pointer until the new entry has been flushed; full crash/reboot qualification remains a release gate. There are no login, logout or enrollment commands in this delivery. When authentication is designed, revisit session-to-policy identity binding, account/organization switching, logout invalidation, credential lifecycle, authenticated refresh and CI identity, plus end-to-end server interoperability. Configuration policy is not a login session and does not grant publishing/signing authority. Connector credentials, shell secrets, verified tool installation and remote action caching also remain separate integrations.

The implementation status records tested revisions and host coverage. The current contracts have focused coverage in resolution and editing tests, CLI tests, execution enforcement tests, and signed managed-policy tests. Agent transition tests beside the policy agent cover key rotation, elapsed deadlines and denial/clock behavior. These tests do not establish interoperability with a production authenticated service. Documentation structure is checked with node tooling/check-docs.mjs; that check does not validate product behavior. The quick-start command sequence and the provisioned-Node task example were separately exercised against the compiled CLI on Windows during this documentation update.

The project environment reference documents env._.path, its atomic replacement and file-relative paths. The optional compatibility capability is config.env-path/v1. This metadata is not exported into task/build environments.

Global verbosity and OYZU_LOG are typed invocation-only presentation inputs, resolved before any project session. They are not project keys and never enter effective execution snapshots or configuration digests. Explicit CLI controls override the complete environment filter. Help/version do not resolve it. See CLI diagnostic controls for grammar and errors.

[tools] declarations can also be written, replaced and removed with oyzu install SPEC, oyzu uninstall and -g/--local/--profile, which keep comments and lock the result; see tool commands. A declaration is a version string, or mise's option-table form with only a version key (node = { version = "22" }), which validation normalizes to that string so every consumer sees one form. Edits change only the table's version. Any other option key, or a table without a version string, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the key; see option tables. tools.platforms is an optional project/profile string set consumed through the normal configuration cascade. It restricts Rust lock metadata coverage, not the artifact matrix or installation authority. When absent, pin uses the finite default metadata platforms. An empty or unsupported selection fails pin. Values are exact OS/architecture/ABI tuples; this setting is not a tool version request. No schema version changes.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/direct-tests.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu run test produces a test-only dist/ bundle for single-package Node projects and native npm/pnpm/Yarn workspaces using node:test, Jest, Vitest or Mocha, Python projects using pytest through pip, uv or Poetry, Go modules/workspaces using native testing, Helm charts using local validation and optional helm-unittest suites, Rust apps/workspaces using nextest and Cargo doctests, supported Ant assertion/JUnit targets, native Maven reactors, and Gradle multi-project/composite builds. Native dependencies and any required reporters must already be installed. Node itself is resolved during oyzu build preflight when the project has no pin (see below); oyzu run uses an existing selection. There is no Docker, desktop, sign-in or tool-installation prerequisite for this host workflow. See Python test reporting, Go testing and Helm testing for native prerequisites and coverage scope; the examples below use Node. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist oyzu run test -- --test-name-pattern=greeting The builder recognizes the conventional runner or a supported exact test command and supplies native JUnit and applicable application coverage reporting. Helm records coverage as inapplicable, with one local-validation report and a separate native unittest report when detected. Host Helm tests require prepared chart dependencies, a provisioned Helm executable and the helm-unittest plugin when suites are selected. Their orchestration is compiled into Oyzu and requires no Python interpreter; they do not install tools or download dependencies. Existing npm pretest/posttest lifecycle behavior stays native. Qualified names such as api:test use that target's configuration and working directory; Oyzu pre_/post_ hooks and declared prerequisites follow the task engine's ordering. Forwarded arguments apply only to the requested task.

The invocation uses the same report binding, validation, collection and bundle transaction as captured builds. dist/manifest.json links current JUnit and coverage reports (LCOV for Node, Cobertura for Python, native statement profiles for Go), their summaries, the recorded plan, execution envelope and logs. It records no newly built application artifacts and does not run packaging, lint or formatting just because tests were requested. Use oyzu build for builder stages and snapshot artifacts. Local text-mode tasks inherit stdin and tee stdout/stderr live to the caller and the bundle's numbered log files, including on native failure. The child's output streams are pipes. An explicitly interactive = true task instead inherits real stdout/stderr descriptors in text mode; its output cannot also be retained and its bundle stdout/stderr logs are empty. JSON mode captures both streams even for interactive tasks, without terminal output descriptors. Native report files and their validation remain required independently of stream capture. See development task streams for empty-stdout checks, quiet mode, completion waiting and current verification limits. Native test failures, missing required reports, malformed reports and an unmet configured coverage minimum fail the command. Valid failed-test reports and bounded malformed report bytes are retained when available. Collection waits for the post-hook so that a report-transforming hook can finish. A failing pre-hook blocks its test; a failing test skips its success-only post-hook; a failing post-hook retains the test's available reports. A launch failure produces failed action evidence rather than success. Unexecuted actions are marked blocked. Default reports use a fresh private directory for every invocation. Custom commands are not parsed as arbitrary shell programs or replaced with guessed native commands. Hooks and commands receive OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT for concrete assigned paths.

oyzu build and oyzu run <target>:test resolve the same task: an explicit Oyzu task, else the project's native package.json test script, else the builder default. Discovering a script does not by itself add it to the build lifecycle. The resolved task has one of three integration modes, shown in the human summary and in extensions."oyzu.dev/report-integration": builder-default: no native test override; the builder runs node --test with JUnit and lcov reporters, and the Node runner and coverage need no extra packages. native-runner: a package.json script that is exactly node --test followed only by plain --flag options. The script still runs through npm, so project config and pretest/posttest lifecycle behavior stay native and tests run once; reporter and coverage options are appended after --. Scripts that name paths, their own reporters, coverage or watch options are not instrumented, because flags after paths are silently ignored by Node. opaque: any other command is preserved verbatim, with nothing appended or guessed. Supported reports are collected only if the command writes them to the assigned OYZU_TEST_REPORT / OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT locations (or a declared reports path) during this execution. Absent reports are recorded as status: missing. Each test action also produces a test-evidence record (manifest.extensions."oyzu.dev/test-evidence", the Test evidence block in human output and evidence in oyzu run --json outcomes) with separate command, test-results and coverage status, and an acceptance verdict: Case Outcome Builder default, reports collected accepted Native override, reports collected accepted Opaque command passed, reports absent, not required incomplete: "command passed; test results missing; coverage missing"; the build still succeeds Test command failed (any mode) command fails; partial reports are retained; rejected Report missing and required (checks.required = ["tests"] or ["coverage"], checks.coverageMinimum, or an explicit task reports entry) report-missing error diagnostic; command fails; rejected Builder default but a report is missing fails Only reports produced by the current execution can satisfy a requirement; stale files are rejected. Oyzu does not edit package.json or checked-in configuration. A literal declaration can also redirect a supported exact command: [tasks."project:test"] argv = ["node", "--test"] reports = [{ kind = "test", format = "junit", path = "reports/junit.xml" }] The path is relative to the task's working directory. Oyzu creates missing parent directories for literal paths. A report declaration does not remove the other required report kinds. Explicit report paths or globs must have no existing matching output before the invocation; preserve or remove earlier files before rerunning. Oyzu fails rather than treating stale evidence as current. For a glob, the command remains responsible for producing matching files and directories; no single output path environment variable is inferred for multiple files.

Host tasks often build into dist/ before running tests. Direct tests preserve those files alongside their new evidence, recording paths, sizes and digests under extensions.oyzu.dev/host-outputs. Previous artifact bytes are preserved as ordinary host output; they are not listed as artifacts produced by this test invocation. Inspection verifies the preserved inventory. Earlier Oyzu reports, evidence and logs stay in history rather than becoming current test results. The previous directory moves to .oyzu/history/<new-run-id> through the shared transaction. Native output must use portable regular files/directories; links, reparse points and collisions with new evidence fail. manifest.json, plan.json, envelope.json and logs are reserved bundle paths. An application-owned manifest or other reserved-path collision needs to be preserved or relocated before this workflow can finalize. Failures during preflight or output preservation can leave the earlier bundle in place; check the command outcome and run identity instead of assuming any existing dist belongs to the latest attempt. See bundle retention and recovery.

The plan, envelope and manifest disclose oyzu.dev/invocation with kind: test, execution: host, isolation: none, source: observed-before-run and toolIdentity: unverified. Source identity is observed before executing against the live checkout; dependencies, ambient tools and subsequent source mutations are not captured. Actions declare network: host, are not cacheable, and disclose that sandbox resource limits are not enforced. Environment values in plan records are redacted. Native output/logs remain the output of the invoked programs; they are not a general secret-redaction service. CI detection gives ci-unverified, not a trusted producer identity. Effective configuration identity and available management metadata are recorded, but this test invocation does not satisfy unrelated full-build checks or grant publication/signing authority. Inspection checks integrity and agreement of invocation records, not authenticity. This is local development evidence, not hermetic or production provenance. Integrated profiles are single-package Node tests and npm workspaces (node:test, Jest, Vitest and Mocha), Python's pytest default, native Go module/workspace tests and Helm charts. Rust app/workspace native acceptance passed on all three CI hosts as described below. Ant tests and Maven reactor tests connect their native test and JaCoCo adapters to this collector. Gradle composite tests also supply named native reports. pnpm/Yarn workspace tests now use native membership with the shared package collector. Docker still lacks this test-only bundle integration. A supported test depending on an unsupported test profile fails before execution rather than claiming complete evidence for both. These are implementation gaps; the intended common builder reporting contract remains broader. The native probe is python tooling/test-direct-test-bundles.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path>, with dependencies from tooling/design-requirements.txt. It checks real native tests, application coverage, lifecycle behavior, hooks, failed/missing/malformed evidence, redirected/stale reports, launch failures, native output preservation, history and inspection tampering. CI runs it after CLI compilation on Windows, macOS and Linux. Revision-specific results and remaining gaps are recorded in implementation status; CI wiring alone does not prove all hosts passed. python tooling/test-helm-direct.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --helm <helm-path> exercises application and root library charts, qualified targets/hooks, native unittest, failed reports, coverage inapplicability and bundle inspection. The probe requires Helm 3.22.0, helm-unittest 1.2.0 and Python 3.11+; Python runs this repository's verification harness, not the product's Helm orchestration. The shared TaskPlan carries coverage applicability into target records, including after post-hooks; a positive coverage minimum cannot be satisfied by a chart without a coverage report. The Linux Helm suite runs this probe after downloading the compiled CLI. Windows native results and pending Linux execution are recorded in implementation status; macOS native execution is not yet qualified.

Jest 29.7.0, Vitest 5.0.3 with matching @vitest/coverage-v8 5.0.3, and Mocha 11.8.0 with c8 10.1.3 are exercised by the direct framework probe. Provision project dependencies before oyzu run test. Mocha requires project-installed c8 10.x or explicitly provisioned fallback tools via OYZU_NODE_REPORTING_HOME; see Mocha reporting. Tests do not install missing reporters. Vitest's declared coverage provider must match its version; other framework major versions are not qualified by these checks. No test section is needed. Detection selects the implicit runner; exact native scripts (jest, jest --ci, vitest, vitest run, mocha) keep npm pretest/posttest behavior while the existing framework adapter adds JUnit and LCOV. Native configuration remains authoritative for test selection, reporters and coverage scope. Both implicit and scripted tests use the common bundle collector, with native failures retained in the manifest. Recognized command overrides retain report obligations; arbitrary script bodies must supply their assigned reports themselves. The framework wrappers resolve npm to its provisioned JavaScript entrypoint, preserving argument arrays and avoiding shell-dependent .cmd invocation on Windows. They retain native npm configuration. The three-platform CI probe covers implicit runners and npm scripts; pnpm/Yarn scripted host combinations are not yet qualified by this probe. Host tests retain ambient network access as disclosed in the invocation; they do not establish hermetic build evidence. Run python tooling/test-node-framework-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> after npm ci in tooling/fixtures/jest, tooling/fixtures/vitest, tooling/fixtures/mocha and tooling/images/node-quality, with tooling/design-requirements.txt installed. It invokes the real CLI and native frameworks, validates JUnit/LCOV bundles, checks native/Oyzu hook ordering and failed assertions, and calls oyzu inspect dist. Fixture copies preserve npm's executable symlinks: dereferencing Unix .bin entries breaks Vitest's relative imports before the native test command can run. The initial Linux/macOS probe exposed that harness error. The corrected probe passed on all three hosts at bfa2b7c in run 37049720609. npm workspace report ownership and native prerequisites are described in npm workspaces; pnpm/Yarn direct workspace integration is described in native workspace tests; Yarn and pnpm captured workspace builds are now implemented with isolated CLI acceptance pending. Rust app/workspace direct tests use the same collector with nextest JUnit, Cobertura and doctest invocation reports. The direct reporting step passed on Windows MSVC, Linux and macOS at bfa2b7c. The local Windows GNU toolchain lacks the required profiler runtime. See Rust prerequisites and current verification for measured scope and unsupported combinations. Workspace bundle publication holds an invocation lock through finalization and rollback. Completing or abandoning the transaction explicitly unlocks it so a transient inherited Unix file description cannot keep the next invocation locked out. Concurrent active invocations still fail with the workspace-lock diagnostic; this does not permit concurrent writes to one bundle.

With no configuration pin, oyzu build preflight requests lts whether or not engines.node is present: it selects the greatest release whose Node index lts field is a non-empty string and that satisfies every engine constraint. If no LTS release satisfies them, it falls back to the greatest stable release satisfying them; the requirement reason in the plan explains this fallback rule. With 24.x marked LTS and 26.x Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 selects 26.x. Configuration pins, including latest, 26, exact versions and lts/<name>, keep their existing behavior and must satisfy engines. Preflight writes oyzu.lock and installs the selection before any action runs; it prepares tools only and never runs tests. See Node selection. oyzu build --connector-bindings <file> supplies host bindings for administrator-routed tool sources. .nvmrc/.node-version are not read yet. python tooling/test-node-test-reporting.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> [--store <dir>] [--lock <oyzu.lock>] creates temporary Git fixtures and runs oyzu build --full and oyzu run site:test for: builder default, native node --test --test-concurrency=1 with pretest/posttest (each runs once per invocation), opaque wrapper, a cooperative wrapper, failing default and native tests, and an opaque wrapper with checks.required = ["tests"]. It asserts the integration mode, per-capability statuses, acceptance verdict, retained partial reports and the report-missing diagnostic. Qualification limits are recorded in implementation status.

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/discovery-selection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. Static discovery decides each exclusive role of a Node or Python target, such as its package manager or formatter, from native project files. It reads bounded metadata, never runs a tool, script or configuration file, and never breaks a tie silently. When native evidence settles a role, no Oyzu configuration is needed. When it does not, discovery fails and names both the conflicting inputs and the build.yaml declaration that settles the role. oyzu build --plan shows every decision with its reason.

Without build.yaml, discovery selects a native project at the root or searches below that root for targets. The inventory walk stops descending as soon as it finds a target; the selected native builder owns discovery within that target. Nested Git repositories and directories with their own build.yaml also stop the walk. Existing generated/dependency directory exclusions, the depth limit of 32 and the limit of 1,024 targets still apply. Ordinary files below an already selected target do not add inventory traversal work. These rules apply equally to human and JSON discovery output. The invocation's configuration boundary also bounds conventional target discovery. An empty or malformed ancestor .git marker does not select that ancestor as a workspace: for standalone sibling projects with no enclosing Oyzu configuration, oyzu -C first run list discovers only first's tasks. In a real Git workspace, discovery still includes its conventional targets, and an unqualified task exposed by several targets remains ambiguous. Use the target-qualified task named by the error, or --root first when deliberately selecting a narrower root. Gitdir-pointer repositories and linked worktrees follow the same boundary rules. Each detector reports a candidate with evidence of one strength. The strongest evidence wins: Strength Examples declared a test script that runs exactly one recognized test runner native a lockfile, package.json packageManager, a framework configuration file, a pyproject.toml tool table conventional a declared dependency, a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml, a uv.lock that locks no packages default the documented default when nothing else applies, such as npm, ESLint, Prettier, pip or Ruff Two different candidates with the strongest evidence are a conflict. A candidate the builder has no adapter for, such as packageManager: nub@0.8.3, is unsupported. Both fail discovery; neither registration order nor file order picks a winner. Native rules that settle a role without configuration: Lockfiles beat a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml. pnpm reads settings from pnpm-workspace.yaml and can write the file on its own; only its packages list declares a workspace (the pnpm adapter already treats a settings-only file as no workspace). A file without packages is conventional pnpm evidence, so package-lock.json (npm) outranks it, while with no lockfile it still selects pnpm over the npm default. A file with packages, or one that is not a YAML mapping, stays native and conflicts with another manager's lockfile. The runner a compound test script names. When the test script is not exactly a recognized command (jest, vitest run, mocha, ...) but its &&, ||, ; and | segments name exactly one of jest, vitest, mocha or node --test, that runner is declared evidence. Segments such as pnpm lint, npm run unit or yarn unit are followed into the referenced package script. Leading NAME=value assignments, cross-env, npx and <manager> exec are skipped. A script with quotes, $, backticks, parentheses, redirection or manager flags such as --filter is not read; its framework is then decided by the remaining evidence. The script itself still runs natively, without report instrumentation unless it is an exact recognized command. A uv.lock that locks no packages. uv records the project itself in uv.lock, so a lock without any [[package]] cannot belong to this project's manager. It is conventional evidence and yields to poetry.lock or [tool.poetry]. A uv.lock that does lock packages stays native.

When discovery fails, declare the target and add the selector the error names under with: pytest: uses: python/package with: formatter: ruff If native files identify more than one builder, select uses first. For example, the pinned Mermaid root contains both package.json and Dockerfile; its build.yaml needs mermaid: {uses: node/app} before the Node test-runner decision can be made. That choice does not require a with.test-framework selector: pnpm lint && vitest run selects Vitest from the native test script. Builder with key Values node/app, node/package package-manager npm, pnpm, yarn test-framework node-test, jest, vitest, mocha, custom linter eslint, biome formatter prettier, biome python/app, python/package, python/library package-manager pip, uv, poetry linter ruff, flake8 formatter ruff, black The keys match the role names in --plan and in the target's oyzu.dev/discovery plan extension. A selection wins over every observation; discovery still records the observations, and the selected value must be one of the listed values. Any other value, a non-string value or any other with key fails. A selection applies to the declared target's own root only; it does not change the decisions of packages inside a Node workspace. Tool versions are not selected here: they belong in oyzu.toml. Example errors: conflicting Python formatter candidates black, ruff: black via pyproject.toml tool.black; ruff via pyproject.toml tool.ruff; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {formatter: black}` or `with: {formatter: ruff}` conflicting Node package manager candidates nub, pnpm (nub unsupported): nub via package.json /packageManager; pnpm via pnpm-lock.yaml lockfile; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {package-manager: pnpm}` The suggestions list the supported candidates that were observed; when none was, they list every supported value. Selecting a manager or runner the project does not natively use can still fail later, in that tool's own preparation or test run.

oyzu build --plan shows a Discovered table per target with each role, the selected candidate and the reason. With --json, each entry of targets has a discovery object mapping the role to selected and reason. For example: package-manager npm native package-lock.json lockfile; outranks pnpm (conventional pnpm-workspace.yaml settings without packages) formatter ruff build.yaml with.formatter; discovery also observed black A reason names the strength and evidence of the winner and every candidate it outranked with non-default evidence. Executed builds keep the complete observations, detector registry and any selector in the plan's oyzu.dev/discovery extension.

The Rust builder reads rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain in every form rustup accepts: the legacy rust-toolchain file holding only a toolchain name, such as nightly-2020-07-10, stable or 1.95.0; the TOML [toolchain] table, in either file, with channel (stable, beta, nightly, <major.minor>, <major.minor.patch>, optionally dated or with a host triple), components, targets and profile; a table without channel, which rustup resolves to the default toolchain: Oyzu then uses its own default (the [tools] rust selection in oyzu.toml, otherwise the adapter baseline) and keeps the declared components, targets and profile; path, a local toolchain directory. Oyzu cannot provision it, so oyzu pin and build tool resolution fail with toolchain.path names the local toolchain ...; select a Rust release in oyzu.toml with [tools] rust = "<version>". An explicit [tools] rust overrides it. An empty [toolchain] table, channel together with path, or an empty or whitespace-containing channel fails. Both files together still fail with both rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain exist, although rustup itself prefers rust-toolchain. Reading a channel is not resolving it: the Rust tool backend currently resolves exact three-part stable versions, and other channels report that backend version selection is needed.

Selections are read once, at discovery, from the frozen build.yaml inventory. Captured workspace planning reuses the target's decisions for its root. The host development composition of npm workspace tests and quality checks re-detects each package, including the root, without them, so a root that needed a selection fails there. Node output profiles and the Python test framework have no selector. The six discovery stops in the feasibility corpus are covered by fixtures in tests/integration/discovery.rs; the shared resolver by discovery::detectors unit tests; Rust toolchain forms by builders::rust::requirement_evidence unit tests. The pinned-corpus qualification records a compiled-CLI Windows plan against all six real source commits, including required selector reruns and its limits. It does not qualify builds or other host platforms.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/local-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The current implementation connects host-native Cargo, Go applications, npm dist applications and pip wheel builds to the local development proposal. Qualification is recorded by scenario in the tool user-flow record. Do not interpret the commands below as completed qualification of every platform or build mode. The host coordinator also admits existing captured docker/image workers, with per-target placement shown by --plan. See image workers and qualification limits. Host processes remain unrestricted; worker enforcement does not extend to the entire graph. BuildKit actions supervise both the docker exec client and the worker. A nonzero client exit reports BUILDKIT_BUILDCTL_FAILED; a stopped, OOM-killed or unreachable worker reports BUILDKIT_WORKER_UNAVAILABLE. Container state and daemon probes run every five seconds with individual two-second deadlines; the final check runs immediately when the client exits. An observed stopped or OOM-killed container fails immediately. Failed inspection or daemon probes need three consecutive failures; a successful check resets the count. A dead daemon therefore does not wait for the action timeout. Diagnostics retain the buildctl exit code/signal when available, container exit and memory limit. State.OOMKilled confirms OOM; exit 137 alone is reported as possible OOM or external SIGKILL. If the Docker client is still stuck, its exit is explicitly unavailable. Cleanup has a separate five-second bound. Retry after restoring the worker or providing enough memory; failed actions do not publish artifacts.

oyzu pin --dry-run previews requirements and lock changes without installing native tools or changing project files. For a new project or a version-1 resolution lock it resolves compiler metadata; --offline requires matching cached metadata. oyzu pin publishes complete resolutions, with conflicts and incomplete inputs reported as failures. See tool planning. All project locks use one version-1 contract. pin resolves requirements whether or not installation records already exist, and preserves those records when publishing resolutions. Incomplete resolution leaves the lock unchanged. Build preflight installs missing supported pinned tools; native host prerequisites still require external provisioning. Pinning itself does not install tools. When a selected builder admits automatic tool resolution and the project has no oyzu.lock, native build preflight resolves its requirements and publishes the lock without editing authored TOML. It captures the published lock before installing and activating the exact selection for native actions. This uses the normal acquisition verification and installation leases; an ambient compiler is not required for supported managed tool requirements. Existing locks remain frozen: incompatible or missing selections require an explicit pin update rather than silently resolving during execution. Offline preparation requires the existing metadata, archive or installation needed by the selected provider. The empty-store qualification and current platform limits are recorded in the fresh-checkout record. The initial adapter covers Rust: rust-toolchain.toml or the legacy rust-toolchain file, Cargo package/workspace rust-version minimums, declared components/targets/profile, and the tools/components required by the existing native build/test/lint/format stages. Every toolchain-file form rustup accepts is read; see Rust toolchain files. A file without channel keeps its components and uses the configured or default Rust; a local path toolchain fails resolution unless oyzu.toml selects a release. Both toolchain filenames together are an error. In the discovery inventory, no toolchain declaration means Rust is reported without a selected version; a build then locks the greatest stable release (pinning is optional). That inventory reports effective Oyzu tool settings separately without claiming resolution. The resolver resolves those inputs through the tool-planning contract described above. Each fact includes its source; repeated facts retain their sources. System linker/SDK requirements are explicit. Windows discovery uses the declared toolchain channel: windows-gnullvm identifies LLVM-MinGW UCRT, Clang linking and a Rust profiler runtime; windows-msvc identifies Microsoft Build Tools and the Windows SDK. A windows-gnu declaration explicitly calls for a coverage-capable alternative. An unqualified channel such as 1.95.0 lists GNU/LLVM and supported MSVC as alternatives, rather than assuming the user's rustup default. This static discovery does not run rustup, inspect PATH or install Windows components. Dependency build-script requirements, compiler/profile compatibility and inherited parent-directory toolchain files are not inferred in this slice. Node requirements are also resolved through the shared tool contract. For the native pip wheel path, CPython is resolved from requires-python or .python-version and installed from Python Build Standalone (details); uv, Poetry and legacy Python tools are not provisioned. Other unsupported requirements remain explicit. The command works offline in standalone mode; existing configuration loading and managed policy rules still apply. Pinning currently requires the workspace root. On 2026-10-03 the compiled discovery implementation inspected this checkout's requirements with PATH empty. Two integration tests passed for toolchain-free inspection, unchanged lock bytes and conflicting manifest rejection. Other hosts are unverified. Discovery evidence is available in pin JSON alongside the resolution preview. It is not installed-tool evidence. Unsupported prerelease lock versions are rejected; no legacy decoder or automatic migration is provided. Existing tool stores are left intact. See the lock contract.

Native Rust compilation retains compiler state under the original project's .oyzu/native/rust/<host>/, while source compilation runs in a private target projection. The Rust builder explicitly identifies its absolute cache and inventory arguments as host paths, including the separate test cache when quality stages are selected. These exact arguments retain their host locations even when a project is rooted under /workspace/, /out/ or /oyzu/. Captured workspace, output and runtime paths still translate into the source projection, report output and engine runtime. Path declarations do not relax native cache, binary inventory or artifact containment checks. Native Rust builds now project inferred snapshot package versions into the private manifests using the same resolver as captured builds. Each native member keeps its own package scope and tag baseline, augmented by the declared target prerequisite closure. Cargo reconciles only private workspace versions offline against the existing lock, preserving locked external packages. Compiled CARGO_PKG_VERSION, artifact version metadata and plan/manifest decisions use the projected version; executable filenames retain their native names. The original manifests and Cargo/tool locks remain unchanged. Conflicts and missing offline dependencies fail preparation with recovery guidance. This new Rust projection passes the Windows three-application pair with and without a declared producer edge, including native reports and independent compiled-version execution. This does not qualify other hosts or all native profiles; see version inference. This fixes issue #384, where an absolute host cache was mistaken for a captured /workspace/ mount and compilation failed with COMMAND_FAILED: No such file or directory after successful preparation. Retry the same native build with the corrected CLI; no project configuration or cache migration is required. python tooling/test-native-host-paths.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --parent <writable-directory> checks two native binaries, repeat compilation, bundle inspection and unchanged source/configuration files. Use a parent under /workspace/ to exercise the original collision; --full additionally checks native quality-stage cache paths with provisioned test/coverage tools. This does not qualify captured builds or other operating systems.
