documents.t: Native Rust builds now check the selected environment with a temporary, dependency-free Cargo compile-and-link probe before compiling project code. The probe honors Cargo linker configuration and Rust flags; selected test stages also request coverage instrumentation. Success verifies this basic capability, not every library needed by dependency build scripts. Temporary probe files are removed after success or failure. No OS components are installed. oyzu run performs the same probe before starting a Rust task that compiles or links (cargo build, test, install, check, clippy, doc, run, rustc), once per target and after tool preparation. Tasks that compile nothing, such as cargo fetch, skip it. Without a linker the task fails in under a second with the guidance below instead of a raw compiler error; a windows-gnullvm toolchain is told to put LLVM-MinGW's bin directory on PATH. Oyzu does not install LLVM-MinGW. A failure reports EXECUTOR_PREREQUISITE_UNAVAILABLE with the native cause and external provisioning guidance. Correct the selected toolchain/linker/SDK and rerun. Discovery and pinning remain static and report availability as not checked; only actual preflight executes the probe. Managed tools and executor prerequisites are separate categories in the inventory. Compile-only inventory omits automatic quality-stage helpers; explicitly declared components remain requirements. This check currently covers native Rust execution. It does not introduce remote executor probes, arbitrary system-package detection or OS provisioning. A ready host capability is not a claim of hermeticity or publication eligibility. Plain oyzu build selects native development execution when every selected target is native-eligible (Rust, Go, Gradle, Maven, npm node/app and pip Python, plus admitted image workers). Other builder/workspace shapes retain their existing captured behavior. oyzu build --isolated explicitly uses the existing captured container executor; --image also retains that path. --affected computes its selection first and then follows the same native-eligibility rules as a plain build, falling back to the captured path only where a plain build would. A failed native or isolated build never retries through another executor. CI detection does not change this selection. Plain local builds need pinned Rust/Cargo and provisioned native compilation prerequisites. Preflight verifies or installs the pinned tools before native dependency preparation. Declared platform relationships and target selection are validated before automatic pinning acquires tool metadata or publishes a lock. Invalid or ambiguous matrix relationships therefore fail without starting tool provisioning. Quality stages additionally need their tools: rustfmt for formatting, Clippy for linting, and nextest, cargo-llvm-cov and the compiler's LLVM tools/profiler runtime for tests with coverage. The Rust test prerequisites describe report tooling. Native dependency preparation first checks the Cargo cache and acquires missing locked inputs when online, as described below. The existing historical Windows coverage qualification includes the MSVC toolchain/linker/SDK. The locally provisioned windows-gnu 1.95 compiler failed a coverage probe with missing profiler_builtins on 2026-10-03. A separate Rust 1.95 x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm experiment on 2026-10-04 passed two tiny-project tests through cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 and nextest 0.9.146, producing a Cobertura report with five of six lines covered using LLVM-MinGW UCRT 20260616 and Clang linking. The compiled CLI also passed oyzu run test on that probe; oyzu inspect dist confirmed both tests and the same collected coverage counts. This required no Microsoft Build Tools installation. It proves direct test and coverage execution, not the complete Oyzu self-build or automatic tool provisioning. The full Oyzu checkout also passed cargo check --locked --offline --bin oyzu with GNU/LLVM, Clang and native CMake/Ninja; final executable linking was not tested by that check. Coverage remains required when the test/coverage stage is selected; plain local compilation does not select it automatically. The native path builds development-profile binaries. Plain local oyzu build automatically schedules compilation only. oyzu build --full, detected CI context or the CI profile also schedule test/JUnit/coverage/doctest integration, Clippy and read-only formatting checks. Explicit checks.required, coverage minimums, hooks and task prerequisites remain enforced in fast mode. Binaries are collected only after the selected stages succeed. oyzu run test, oyzu run lint and oyzu run format-check remain explicit task entry points. Native build overrides are currently rejected with an explicit diagnostic. Ordinary hooks and task prerequisites use the shared task graph. Required configuration checks remain enforced; unsupported managed host execution fails before native preparation. This repository sets Cargo's development and test profiles to debug = 0, omitting generated debug information while retaining debug assertions. The development profile optimizes the direct SHA-256 dependency (sha2 0.10.9) at level 3; the test profile inherits that package override. Oyzu's own code and other dependencies retain their existing optimization settings. This reduces the CPU cost of full tool-payload and evidence hashing without caching or skipping verification. Dependency upgrades must keep this version-specific override aligned with the direct sha2 dependency. Release settings are unchanged. Windows worker tests relaunch their own test executable; embedded debug information previously grew that executable beyond the worker's 512 MiB image limit and caused TOOL_WORKER_IMAGE_INVALID before launch. Source-level debugger information is unavailable in these default builds. Profile overrides that restore debug information can reintroduce this failure; rebuild with the repository defaults to recover. The image limit, integrity checks, test/report gates and scenario timeouts remain unchanged. Other projects retain their own native Cargo profile settings. --all-platforms requests the declared matrix through the existing captured executor; it requires its provisioned Docker environment. Native execution does not cross-compile or confer production publication eligibility. Native development output is a runnable binary, not a versioned source distribution; use the isolated path for the existing packaging contract. Its manifest record still carries the bundle's required version: the builder's own artifact version where it has one, otherwise the target's resolved version. A consumer that declares a platform other than the host, such as a docker/image with platforms: [linux/amd64] that materializes a Go binary on a Windows host, does not use the native path, because native producers are built for the host only. Plain oyzu build (and --plan) then selects the captured executor, which builds each producer for the platform its consumer requires, so the binary is a Linux executable. When the consumer's platform is the host's, the native path is unchanged. A pinned Go, Node or helm is restored from the lock in that captured worker (see Go, Node and Helm); any other pinned tool the worker cannot yet take from the lock is still refused there.

oyzu build --plan previews the same execution-path selection as a build: local host when supported, otherwise the captured executor. --isolated, --all-platforms, named targets, profiles and --full keep their normal selection meaning. The preview itself needs neither Cargo nor Docker installed. The preview reads configuration and native manifests, applies the shared target, matrix and task-selection rules, and shows each target's discovery decisions with their reasons, selected/skipped stages, declared task ordering and consolidated tool requirements. See discovery decisions and selectors. It does not install tools, fetch packages, execute build tools or project scripts, create a lock, open a tool store, write a source snapshot, or create/replace a build bundle. Application dependencies are acquired only by an actual build's preparation. --affected additionally hashes local source and reads the local Git baseline using Git; its existing conservative fallback rules still apply, with no network or checkout writes. A preview is deliberately incomplete: installed-tool availability, executor capabilities, dependency cache readiness, exact commands, native-generated stages, artifact names and report bindings remain unresolved. A selected stage means configuration requests it, not that its prerequisites have passed. Dynamic target relationships may add work during real preparation. Success means the static preview was produced; it does not certify build success or publication eligibility. Live build output shows one plan table once, before work starts: targets by stages with run, skip or - cells and one footnote per skip reason. A single target built for several platforms pivots to one row per platform; above twelve rows targets with identical stages share a counted row (-v lists every target). See Result output. Matrix expansion (--all-platforms, --isolated) can yield targets that differ only by platform. In the live build output a single target built for several platforms is one plan table with a row per platform; the requirements table shows "all N targets" when every target shares a requirement. --json still reports every target individually. Targets whose plans differ keep their own sections. Human output uses stage/requirement tables with semantic color on capable terminals (or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1); NO_COLOR preserves plain text. Owned styling is emitted once, after escaping project-controlled values. --json returns a version-1 build-preview record with resolved: false, selection, targets (each with a discovery map of role to selected and reason), tasks, requirements, unresolved details, effect flags and timings. It is not the executable build-plan retained by actual builds in dist/plan.json. The former captured --plan behavior that acquired dependencies is superseded; use an actual build and its retained plan for execution-level evidence. No schema version was bumped. timings reports where the preview spent its wall-clock time, in milliseconds: totalMs and phases, in order discovery (configuration and target discovery), selection (selection, variants, task graph and requirements), source (inventorying the working tree for analysis from file metadata; no file is read until analysis asks for it), analysis (with targets, one entry per analyzed target, then finishMs for merging facts and rulesMs for the diagnostic rules) and planning (stage and task listing). source and analysis are absent when analysis is disabled or fails. Timings describe one run only and are never part of the analysis record, which stays identical between runs.

oyzu build --remote --plan previews what oyzu build --remote would run on a platform pool, without contacting the platform or needing its settings or token. It is the same read-only preview with the pool's selection: isolated execution, full checks, and the ordinary isolated platform selection. --remote does not imply --all-platforms or introduce additional platform variants. Named targets and --affected <base> select as the remote run does; --affected compares with the merge base of <base> and HEAD. The record's execution is remote. The platform's planner runs this command with the project's pinned Oyzu on a checkout of the exact commit to learn each job's requirements before it is queued. The preview reads the working tree, so local uncommitted changes are included even though a remote run never sends them. --isolated, --all-platforms, --image, --check and --download are refused with --remote. Every preview target carries these placement facts: Field Meaning platform The artifact platform. From the target's variant when it declares one; otherwise the executor's own platform decides, shown as unresolved until executor selection. platformSource variant, executor or host (a development-mode host target). executionPlatform The platform an executor must run on, or null when any executor works. A Rust cross-compile runs on linux/amd64 whatever it targets. A Docker image needs its own platform when its reachable final stage has RUN; a clearly independent final stage ignores RUN in unused earlier stages. Ambiguous stage relationships retain the conservative whole-file requirement. needsDaemon, daemonReason Whether the selected work needs a Docker engine on the executor, and why. false for development-mode host targets, Node targets that can use the daemonless sandbox, and admitted image assembly with only its native build task selected. Selected quality tasks or hooks can make an image target require Docker. isolation What the executor must provide to run the target: host (development mode), crun (Linux with unprivileged user namespaces, or a Docker engine), in-process (Oyzu's native OCI assembly and output copy), or docker (a Docker engine). id, logicalTarget, variant Concrete target ID, its original logical name, and its expanded axes. IDs may be normalized and hashed; clients must use the returned ID rather than construct one. A logical dependency waits for every selected variant; a concrete dependency names that variant only. dependsOnTargets Concrete declared ordering and artifact-input dependencies. Cross-target tasks[].dependsOn edges also contribute to the graph. sliceable Whether the static preview finds no reason this target cannot be reused by another slice. false means include it in the consumer's slice, not a separate handoff producer. Runtime preparation, invalid output writes or storage failures can still prevent reuse. sliceReason, sliceDetail Stable refusal code and human explanation when sliceable is false; otherwise null. Codes: ALWAYS_RUN_HOOK, UNCACHED_TASK, UNSCOPED_INPUTS, UNBOUNDED_OUTPUTS, SECRET_ENVIRONMENT, CACHE_DISABLED, SOURCE_PROJECTION. Platforms are written in OCI form (linux/amd64, darwin/arm64), as variants and pool facts name them; a development-mode host target reports the host that way too. OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 does not alter preview selection or placement facts. Plan-only requests never enable the execution guard. Remote planning needs no credentials. Hooks always run, including hooks declaring outputs. Authored tasks need both cache = true and valid declared outputs; inputs outside their target cannot be cache scoped. Static analysis can identify native stages with unbounded outputs (omitted with --no-analysis). Secret environments and disabled local caching prevent storage. Image builders currently use source projections the action cache declines to store. sliceable describes upstream reuse, not whether a target may execute as a slice. Failed builds and runtime output-contract violations are not predictable by this read-only preview and still fail downstream reuse safely. The top-level placement object names which facts are final and which can grow. Each target's platform, executionPlatform and needsDaemon are final, as are the tool requirements of targets whose requirement status is discovered. The selected targets, the task graph, each target's stages and the requirements of unsupported targets can grow: dynamic target relationships found during preparation can add targets, and each added target brings its own facts. The Dockerfile analysis uses the Docker builder's native assembly grammar to identify a clearly independent final stage. Unsupported syntax, stage references and ambiguous dependencies fall back to a whole-file RUN check, which can over-require but never under-require native execution.

oyzu build --no-docker, or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 in the environment, is for executors that have no Docker engine, such as a container or Kubernetes pool. In this mode Oyzu runs no Docker command at all. Before anything is prepared or run it works out the same preview as --plan for the build's selection; if any selected target has needsDaemon: true, the build stops with exit status 3 and nothing runs. Any other value of the variable than empty or 0 enables the mode. oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --json {"error":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON: cli need a Docker engine, which this executor does not provide (--no-docker); nothing was run","reason":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON","targets":["cli"],"exitCode":3} Exit status 3 signals a placement mismatch, so a runner can tell it from a failed build (1) or a refused invocation (2) and requeue the job on a pool that has Docker. Placement normally comes from --remote --plan; this is the guard for when that plan was wrong. Node targets run in the daemonless sandbox in this mode. An admitted RUN-free Dockerfile with FROM scratch or a digest-pinned base can build in process with --isolated --no-docker; it needs no crun or user namespaces. A final stage independent of an unused earlier RUN stage can also use this path; see Docker image assembly. --full selects Dockerfile lint and format checks that still need the Docker worker, so the guard refuses that selection rather than skipping checks. Unsupported Dockerfile work such as RUN also requires Docker. Development builds of host targets run. --no-docker cannot be combined with --remote.

On Linux, the isolated steps of a Node target (npm, pnpm or Yarn) can run under crun, a rootless OCI runtime, instead of docker run. The step gets the same sandbox: no network, a read-only image root, no capabilities, no-new-privileges, a seccomp filter, Docker's masked and read-only /proc paths, the same mounts and the same tmpfs sizes, inside a user namespace that maps the workspace owner to itself. The image's root filesystem is unpacked once per image digest under the image cache and shared by every build on the host. The backend is not part of the action key: both backends produce the same keys and outputs, so a result cached by one serves the other. The build.isolation setting selects the backend: auto (default) uses Docker when an engine answers and crun otherwise, docker always uses Docker, and crun uses crun for Node targets even with Docker present. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun for Node targets whatever the setting says. oyzu install downloads a pinned crun release (1.24), checks its SHA-256 and keeps it in the user data directory; OYZU_CRUN names a crun the executor already provides instead. Images come from their published, digest-pinned source, or from a local Docker engine's copy when one is running; a tag-only local image with no engine has no source and the build fails before running anything. Before running anything, a build that selected crun checks that crun runs and that the host lets an unprivileged process create user, mount, network and PID namespaces. When it cannot, the build stops with NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES, exit status 3 like NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON, naming what failed (for example kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1, a seccomp profile that blocks unshare, or cgroups mounted in hybrid mode). Oyzu never runs the step without the sandbox. {"code":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES","error":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES: the daemonless sandbox (crun) cannot run on this host: cgroups are mounted in hybrid mode, which crun does not support; nothing was run","exitCode":3,"nextStep":"Run on a Linux executor that allows unprivileged user namespaces and has crun, or on one with a Docker daemon.","reason":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES"} crun runs without a cgroup of its own, so the executor pool's limits bound the step rather than per-step memory and CPU limits. Each action in the build manifest records how it was sandboxed in sandbox: backend (docker or crun), the crun runtime version, and resourceLimits (cgroup or pool).

A build can be split into jobs queued along the target graph, each reusing the results its predecessors built. Each job runs a slice: a build of the named targets in which every other target the build needs may only be reused, never built. The pinned worker's private admitted preparation and execution operations use the same executor preflight as ordinary builds: no-Docker refusal, resolved build.isolation selection, then the required sandbox probe before native preparation. They honor the existing OYZU_NO_DOCKER control. A read-only public preview still performs no executor preparation. Private assigned execution emits its completed manifest even when the build fails, then returns the ordinary failure status: 1 for failed/interrupted work, 4 for unavailable upstream reuse or 5 for failed handoff publication. A failed manifest cannot appear to the worker as successful execution. Native admission still requires exact selected records; mismatch diagnostics name the record and changed field names without printing command/environment values. oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci web Input Meaning Target arguments One or several logical target names or concrete preview targets[].id values. A logical name uses the same variant selection as a whole isolated build: runtime variants remain selected, while declared platforms use the normal host filter unless --all-platforms is given. A concrete ID builds exactly that variant, including a non-host platform. Upstream dependencies remain reuse-only unless explicitly named too. --slice-plan <target-id> Requires --slice; repeat once per concrete ID in the original preview, including folded upstreams and unrelated jobs. This is the client contract for inPlan; pass the complete original set unchanged to every slice and retry. Without it, inPlan uses this invocation's selection before preparation and cannot detect growth since an earlier preview. --slice Build only the named targets (at least one is required). Every action of any other target the selection needs (the named targets' depends_on, materialize and task prerequisites, transitively) is looked up in the local cache and the remote tiers; one that is missing fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED instead of running. A slice runs the captured (isolated) path, as pool jobs do. With --plan it prints the isolated preview of that selection, with the same needsDaemon and isolation as --remote --plan. With --no-docker (or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1) it is judged as an isolated build: a Node target runs in the daemonless sandbox, and any other target stops it with NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON (exit 3) before anything runs, so a pool without Docker requeues it rather than failing it. It cannot be combined with --remote, --affected, --check, --no-cache or --verify-contract, and it needs an active action cache when any selected upstream is unnamed. With cache.local = false, naming the entire selection permits a folded slice to run without reuse or handoff writes; an unexpectedly unavailable cache still fails admission. --handoff <oci-url> Requires --slice. The OCI repository (oci://host/path, the same form as cache.remote) read first for upstream results, before cache.ciRemote and cache.remote, and written with every result this slice produces whatever cache.read and cache.write say. The registry decides whether the job may write there, with the credential an ordinary remote uses (OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or the job's ID token). A URL this client cannot use is refused (exit 2) before anything runs. None of these inputs changes a key: a slice derives every upstream key exactly as a whole build does, from the outputs it restores, so per-target slices of a commit produce the same action keys and artifact digests as one whole build. A producer that built something else than this checkout expects therefore shows up as a miss, never as a wrong reuse. The entries are the frozen OEP-0011 entries every remote tier holds; a handoff hit is verified and materialized like any remote hit. Reason codes, each with its own exit status so an executor can act without parsing text: Reason Exit Raised when UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED 4 An action of a target the slice does not build was not restored from any cache. It is recorded as failed, everything that needs its output is blocked, and nothing of it runs. HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED 5 A result of a named target could not be written to the handoff repository (refused, unavailable, or the repository was switched off after an earlier failure). The build is failed even when every action succeeded, because the jobs after it would miss. Exit status 1 stays a failed build and 2 a refused invocation; 3 is NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON or NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES. When both happen, UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED wins. A failed slice prints one JSON line last on stderr, in human and --json mode alike, so an executor that forwards only the tail of the output can act without --json. It has the shape of NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON's error plus the failure's fields (below): {"action":"app:package","error":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED: app:package of upstream target app (key sha256:…) is not in the local cache or oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci; a slice reuses upstream targets and never builds them","exitCode":4,"inPlan":true,"key":"sha256:…","reason":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED","repositories":[{"location":"oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci","status":"active"}],"target":"app","why":null} The build record (dist/manifest.json, printed by --json) carries an oyzu.dev/slice extension: Field Meaning targets The concrete targets this slice built (requested targets and their variants). upstream The other targets it reused. handoff The --handoff location, or null. written One entry per result of a built target that is in the handoff repository: target, action, key and outcome (pushed, converged when an identical entry was already there, conflicts when a different one held the key and was kept). The runs service keeps these on the job, so a later miss can tell a producer that wrote a different key from one that wrote none. misses Every upstream action that was not restored: target, action, key, repositories (each remote asked, with status active or unavailable and why), inPlan, and why when the action was never looked up (for example an authored task without declared outputs, which is never cached). notWritten Every result of a built target that did not reach the handoff repository: target, action, key, repository and status (the registry's answer). failure null, or the first miss (reason: UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED, exitCode: 4) or else the first unwritten result (reason: HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED, exitCode: 5), with that entry's fields. inPlan tests membership in the original set passed with --slice-plan. false means a missing producer was absent from that preview, including a dependency added between preview and execution. That is an explicit plan mismatch; it does not authorize a whole-build replay or repetition of effects that may have occurred. true means an expected producer did not leave a reusable result. Both exit 4; neither permits the slice to execute an unnamed producer. The action cache's summary gains a handoff section beside ciRemote and remote, with the same fields. A result restored from the handoff repository is not a CI result: a later CI build that finds it in its local store looks it up again, as it does for a development remote's. An upstream marked sliceable: false must be named alongside its consumer, for example oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://localhost:5000/demo/ci generate web. If several consumers require its live state or its effects are not known safe to repeat, keep the coupled work in one engine invocation. Transferability and repeatability are separate facts; cache ineligibility does not authorize one execution per consumer. An unnamed unreusable upstream still fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED and its why. Every upstream target is prepared (its dependencies acquired) because its keys include the prepared dependency identity. Verified with the slice-handoff build scenario against zot on Linux (OYZU_ZOT_BINARY=<zot> python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --cli <oyzu> --suite node --only slice-handoff): per-target slices of a two-target project match one whole build key for key and digest for digest with no upstream action run, a deleted upstream entry exits 4, and refused handoff writes exit 5; see implementation status. The expanded scenario adds concrete matrix IDs, folded hooks and graph growth. --suite rust --only slice-corpus adds the pinned serde and regex workspaces, three declared crate targets each, checking every action key and cached output tree digest plus artifact digests from fresh local stores. These additions await execution with Docker; the earlier two-target proof does not qualify them. Invalid configuration, unknown targets and statically invalid relationships fail normally. Configuration is opened offline to preserve the no-network contract; managed configuration that cannot resolve offline fails closed rather than bypassing policy. Correct the reported configuration or run a normal build to perform the preparation needed to resolve remaining details. Native macOS runtime qualification remains pending.

documents.t: Successful binaries are collected in dist/<target>/artifacts/ with their normal native names, then exposed at .oyzu/bin/<name>[.exe]. The shared bundle store retains manifest, plan, envelope, reports and action logs. These disclose host execution, observed source and unverified tool identity; they do not confer production eligibility or assert enforced isolation. Rust state lives under .oyzu/native/rust/<compiler-host>/: target holds native compilation state and tests holds separate instrumented/test state. Cargo owns native invalidation. Prepared package bytes remain in the already provisioned native package cache; this slice does not implement an acquisition proxy, import unmanaged caches as trusted evidence or add a shared artifact cache.

After tool admission, the Rust builder tries locked offline Cargo metadata. If the cache is sufficient, it proceeds without fetching. Otherwise an online build runs cargo fetch --locked through the host executor with live, labeled preflight output, then resolves metadata offline again. Cargo owns registry/Git downloads, checksums and its cache; Oyzu does not rewrite Cargo.lock. Compilation remains offline. oyzu build --offline never takes the fetch path and reports missing inputs with guidance to run an online build or correct the manifest/lock. This is the standalone native path: Cargo uses its configured repositories, credentials and network settings. It is not a broker-controlled acquisition or network isolation guarantee. Managed host tool admission remains unavailable; this does not enable it or change captured-build acquisition. Native preparation failures retain a safe category and recovery guidance even when credential-bearing native details are withheld. Warm-cache qualification alone does not prove cold repository self-building; see the recorded qualification results. Previous claimed artifacts move to bundle history on either successful or failed native builds; unrelated dist files stay protected. See bundle finalization and recovery. Failure returns a nonzero exit and leaves .oyzu/bin at the last successful generation. Treat it as stale relative to the failed attempt. Promotion renames the previous image before replacing the stable name, avoiding direct overwrite of a running Windows image. An image that cannot yet be deleted may remain as a hidden previous generation; repeated Windows self-rebuilds still require proof.

Build the initial executable with cargo build --locked --release --bins, then copy target/release/oyzu[.exe] and target/release/oyzu-shim[.exe] together to a dedicated user PATH directory outside the checkout, preserving any existing installation. This independent fallback must not point back into the compiler output or .oyzu/bin. Check the build exit status before copying, verify the copied binary, and retain a rollback copy. Release builds avoid installing the much larger development/debug executable; the initial release build can be substantially slower than an incremental local build. On Windows, saving a directory in the user PATH does not update an already-open terminal or its parent application. Update the current PowerShell session explicitly, substituting your fallback installation directory: $fallbackBin = 'C:\path\to\oyzu-bootstrap\bin' $env:Path = "$fallbackBin;$env:Path" oyzu --version New terminals inherit PATH from their parent process, so opening another tab in an already-running terminal application may still inherit the older value. The repository configuration contains: [env] _.path = ["./.oyzu/bin"] Activate the shell through the fallback as described in project environments. For PowerShell 7.5+, use oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. Run oyzu build, then _oyzu_hook if an explicit refresh is needed. Get-Command oyzu -CommandType Application (PowerShell), type -P oyzu (Bash), or whence -p oyzu (Zsh) should resolve to the project output. Ordinary oyzu invocations use the activation wrapper, which dispatches to that application; an unqualified command lookup can show the wrapper function instead of its destination. Leaving the project restores the baseline PATH. Merely writing TOML does not activate an existing terminal. Oyzu's repository configures +crt-static for x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm in .cargo/config.toml. This links the compiler's unwind runtime into the Oyzu executables so workers can start without LLVM-MinGW's libunwind.dll on PATH. It does not install an OS component or relax the worker's explicit environment. Other targets retain their native defaults. Compiler flags supplied explicitly through Cargo's environment can override this repository configuration; preserve the static-runtime setting when building this target.

Fresh-store installation and a small native Rust build --full have passed on Windows GNU/LLVM, including automatic helper installation, JUnit and coverage collection, formatting and linting, followed by offline reuse. Use oyzu build --store <path> to select the same store as oyzu install --store <path>. The default remains the shared user store. Relative overrides resolve against the invocation directory (or global --root), before workspace-root discovery. The selected store is used for native installation and verification and captured-build tool preparation; it never changes pins, tool identities, checks or image policy. A missing or invalid installation in that store does not fall back to another store. --offline requires its cached inputs; use the same override on install, build and tool-inspection commands. Repository test fixtures explicitly select their intended profile, and doctest compilation no longer has a private two-minute timeout. Git and Windows PowerShell must be available for the repository's own tests. See commands, measurements and qualification limits. Native execution inherits host capabilities. Cargo's offline mode is not network denial for arbitrary build scripts. New process/network isolation and approved broker routes remain future work. An installed fallback, local successful build or local isolation flag cannot grant production publication authority. Current implementation verification and missing end-to-end evidence are recorded in implementation status. The intended host matrix is Windows/macOS/Linux, but no new host is qualified by this document.

Rust discovers an explicit install task; no custom bootstrap task is needed. See Rust executable installation. With the required tool environment available, run from this checkout: oyzu run install -- --bins --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" The destination is machine-local, not committed task configuration. Windows self-installation stages the Cargo result before replacing the running bootstrap. This invokes Cargo installation, not the full Oyzu build quality gates. Cargo uses release compilation by default; add --debug after -- for a development installation. These profiles use different compiler caches. Run oyzu install first to materialize the pinned native toolchain and its verified installation receipt. An outdated bootstrap can initially be replaced by invoking Cargo directly with the provisioned toolchain: cargo install --path . --bins --locked --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" oyzu run fetch prepares Cargo dependencies; oyzu run install installs project executables; oyzu install provisions development tools. They remain distinct.
