documents.t: The Windows task flow uses a pinned MSVC installation, which needs Visual Studio Build Tools (C++ workload, no IDE) installed first: oyzu pin, oyzu install, then oyzu run install. A checkout whose oyzu.lock was installed with the earlier GNU/LLVM default holds a stale Rust-only installation record that conflicts with the new selection (TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS); delete that oyzu.lock and rerun oyzu pin and oyzu install. Ordinary tool installation does not provision Docker or a Linux worker. Keep machine-specific linker/CMake paths and Cargo cache locations in ignored oyzu.local.toml, using [env] and _.path. Cargo's CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT selects the bootstrap prefix (the binary goes under its bin directory); this setting also applies to oyzu run install. The selected verified Cargo/compiler remain owned by Oyzu, while LLVM/MinGW, CMake and dependency-specific native prerequisites are provisioned separately. Do not commit one developer's absolute machine paths. See native Rust task execution. The Oyzu executable explicitly links its existing unwinder statically on Windows GNU/LLVM. Rust 1.95 otherwise emits a libunwind.dll import, causing startup to fail before CLI code runs when LLVM is absent from PATH. See the upstream Rust explanation. This binary-only link declaration does not change downstream project profiles or install a compiler runtime globally. The local bootstrap retains the provisioned LLVM license next to its installation; packaging remains subject to the existing third-party distribution review, not cleared by this development proof. On Windows, the inferred Oyzu Cargo install task stages installation under the explicit destination root (CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT or forwarded --root). Cargo compiles and installs into staging while the existing bootstrap remains callable. Only after Cargo succeeds does execution publish binaries with Windows file replacement, retaining one .NAME.previous backup per replaced file. Cargo's installation bookkeeping is staged and published too. Cancelling compilation or a native install failure leaves the installed bootstrap unchanged. A forcibly terminated process may leave its private .oyzu-install-* staging directory; do not remove one belonging to an active installation. Publication is per file, not an atomic transaction across the CLI, shim and Cargo metadata. On a publication error, inspect the named file and adjacent backup; close processes still holding an older backup before retrying. Concurrent Oyzu installs to this root serialize; a simultaneous direct Cargo install is outside that coordination. Other packages and non-Windows installs retain native Cargo behavior. Without an explicit root, Oyzu leaves Cargo's destination selection alone and does not move the running executable out of the way. Native builds acquire the same verified configured tool environments as tasks before invoking builder metadata. Leases are retained and reused by all stages with the same frozen target configuration. No tool verification gate is bypassed. Repeated successful native builds replace artifacts recorded by the prior bundle at the newly collected artifact paths. Test-only runs continue preserving those files without claiming them as new build artifacts. Unclaimed native files still cause a collision rather than being overwritten; prior bundles remain in history. Build output starts with Building <directory name> (or Planning for --plan), followed by host platform or the requested matrix, local/isolated execution, and the requested fast/full mode. Relative . paths resolve to the actual directory name. This initial summary does not override configuration or policy; preflight establishes the selected targets and required checks. JSON emits a structured heading event on stderr; quiet mode suppresses it and stdout remains unchanged. Build output follows Preflight → Build → completion summary. Preflight includes configuration, target discovery, pinned tool preparation, native dependency metadata and planning. These internal steps are not competing top-level phases. The default view shows tool, requested version and observed installation status on the same row. Missing tools report acquisition/installation, followed by verification; reused tools report verification before receiving a success mark. The Rust component installer currently reports downloading and installing as a combined step; it does not invent byte percentages. A success mark requires the existing installation verification to finish. Errors stop preflight and remain visible. External SDK/linker prerequisites explicitly remain unchecked until the native tools run; discovering them does not establish availability. Optional formatting, linting, testing and coverage tools are omitted from the fast-build summary unless quality stages are selected. The full declared inventory remains in detailed logs; this presentation does not change pins, installation recipes, enabled stages or enforcement. Additional environment, execution and source context is available with p, rather than repeating it in the default view. Native execution does not imply isolation or verified commit identity. Auto and plain modes use a linear, scrollback-preserving build flow. They do not open an alternate screen or maintain panes. Color is independent of interaction: ui.color=auto colors terminal output unless NO_COLOR is set to a non-empty value; always also colors redirected text and never disables color. A terminal is capable when TERM is not dumb and, on Windows, when the console accepts virtual terminal processing, which the CLI switches on for its own stdout and stderr; a console that refuses gets plain text and no line clears. Active tools and build subprocesses show eight dimmed output lines beneath their headers on capable terminals. Success collapses those lines; failure retains them. Redirected output appends each update. --output interactive retains the old dashboard as an explicit opt-in. JSON remains structured and unstyled; raw child output and retained evidence are unchanged. See build logging. Native builds automatically install missing configured and builder-required tools from existing pins using the shared user store, then verify the selected environment before compiling. Builds never update pinned versions or write a new lock: run oyzu pin for missing or stale resolutions. --offline forbids acquisition and requires the installer's cached inputs. Small terminals retain detailed logs (d) for values outside the visible area. Automatic installation uses the same acquisition, checksum, installation lease and policy checks as oyzu install, consuming the configuration snapshot selected for the build target. Installation errors stop execution before native metadata or compilation. A denied or corrupted selection is not replaced by an unverified PATH tool. This applies to the supported native build path; isolated builds retain their provisioned image contract. Provisioned builds without a portable pin retain their existing behavior. With a portable pin, selected tests include the pinned nextest and cargo-llvm-cov helpers automatically; ordinary fast builds omit them. System linkers and SDKs remain external prerequisites. See helper installation. Native Rust preflight names linker/runtime prerequisites from the selected compiler's reported host (GNU/LLVM, MSVC, MinGW, Apple, or Linux). The actual prepared Cargo environment performs the compile/link probe, including inherited linker configuration and coverage instrumentation when selected. Ready means that probe succeeded using executor-provided facilities; it does not claim that Oyzu installed an OS SDK or independently identified every library's version. Pin's executor table omits tool-version and installation-backend columns because those prerequisites are externally provided and are not probed by pin.

Native host execution records an observed source identity. It validates and hashes source files using the captured-source exclusions, path/type rules and change detection, but does not write an unused temporary source copy. The native compiler still reads the checkout; this does not provide a frozen filesystem or isolation. Captured/container execution still creates its required input copy. Preflight names output-bundle opening, compiler-cache retention, source hashing, CLI identity hashing and report preparation. Each running operation has an explicit completion or failure; report contracts and binding readiness share one completion row. Source and CLI identity completion include measured durations. Slow operations retain named activity updates. See linear logging. The 2026-10-06 provider-identity refresh passed the actual Windows repository bootstrap → pin/install → fast build → local-CLI self-install loop, plus a fresh Linux fixture's install/build/offline/activation flow. See the commands, fixture corrections and limits. Subsequent qualification passed the Windows repository build --full, the Linux repository host build inside Docker, and a deliberate failed-test fixture with retained reports and no published artifacts. See the measured results and cache baseline.
documents.s: Local source evidence and startup progress

documents.t: Native Rust oyzu build retains at most cache.nativeMaxMiB MiB across its selected host's declared compiler caches after normal completion. The default is 8192 MiB (8 GiB). Configure it through the ordinary configuration cascade: [cache] nativeMaxMiB = 8192 Eviction runs Cargo's own cargo clean on the declared cache directory. Oyzu first marks that directory with the standard CACHEDIR.TAG, because current Cargo refuses to clean a target directory without one; a cache created before the tag existed would otherwise fail every build once the budget was exceeded. The setting accepts 1–1048576 MiB, supports ordinary policy numeric constraints, and applies identically online and offline. It is separate from remote result cache preferences. Progress reports the measured size and any reclaimed roots; JSON builds keep those diagnostics on stderr and the result on stdout. The build holds the workspace transaction lock while checking the budget before execution and after collecting artifacts and reports. If over budget, execution runs the selected Cargo's clean --offline --target-dir <validated-directory>. Cargo retains ownership of compiler-file cleanup and its own cache locking. Whole roots are evicted in this order until under budget: the obsolete separate doctest target, coverage target, ordinary build target. Under budget, no native cleanup runs. Doctests now reuse the ordinary build target; instrumentation keeps coverage in a separate target. A budget below the working set trades incremental reuse for space and can cause a cold compile on every invocation. This is a retained-size policy, not a peak disk quota: compilation can temporarily exceed it, and a crash or full disk before collection may leave oversized state until the next invocation. End-of-build cleanup failure emits NATIVE_CACHE_RETENTION_FAILED without discarding build evidence or changing its result; the next pre-build check retries, and a failure there stops execution. Root/entry symlinks and Windows reparse points are rejected rather than followed. Use a normal directory or remove the redirection before retrying. No claim is made of protection against a hostile concurrent filesystem writer. Only builder-declared roots under the selected target's .oyzu/native are eligible. Installed tools, downloads, .oyzu/bin, dist, history/recovery, proof files, other platform roots, direct Cargo's project target, and arbitrary oyzu run tasks are outside this policy. No schema changed and no legacy data was relabeled. The regression entry point is python tooling/test-native-cache-budget.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> with this checkout's pinned Rust/check tools and native linker prerequisites. It proves small-budget rebuilds, retained warm state, doctests, report inspection and failed-build preservation through the compiled CLI.

Run oyzu build or oyzu build --plan from a nested project containing its own build.yaml; no --root is required. Source subdirectories select their nearest ancestor declaration. Repository configuration continues to inherit, while the selected build owns its lockfile and outputs. Parent builds do not automatically include nested build inventories. See configuration boundaries for the configuration contract.

A project whose selected profile has a native host build runs on the machine without Docker: Oyzu resolves missing tools, installs them into the shared store, then invokes the ecosystem's own tools. Other profiles use the isolated executor and fail with a message naming that requirement when Docker is unavailable. Profile Host build Unpinned tool selection Rust (Cargo) Yes Automatic (greatest stable release; must satisfy Cargo rust-version; a rust-toolchain.toml channel or explicit pin wins; see Rust installation) Node node/app with npm and a dist/ output Yes Automatic (greatest LTS satisfying every engines.node constraint; greatest matching stable release if no LTS matches; selection) Go go/app: one module, no go.work, exactly one package main Yes Automatic (greatest stable release satisfying the go directive minimum) Python pip with pyproject.toml Yes (wheel) Automatic (greatest stable CPython satisfying requires-python; see Python installation) Java Maven reactor (readable jar names; a committed mvnw is run) Yes (jars; tests run in verify) Automatic (JDK from the declared level, Maven 3.9 unless a wrapper supplies it; see Java installation) Java Gradle build (a committed gradlew is run; jars from Gradle's model; tests run in build) Yes Automatic (JDK from the declared level, Gradle 8 or 9) Go libraries, workspaces, several binaries; Ant and other Java; uv/Poetry/requirements-only Python; other Node profiles No: isolated executor Not applicable oyzu pin is optional for Rust, Go and Node. With no oyzu.lock, preflight resolves the requirement, writes oyzu.lock and installs from it; commit that file to make later builds reproducible, or delete it to re-resolve. An explicit [tools] go = "1.24" takes precedence. The Go build runs go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o <private output> with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so only the locked toolchain compiles and none is downloaded mid-build, and GOPROXY=off under --offline. Compiler diagnostics are shown with their file and line, the exit status is preserved and no previous binary is republished. The artifact is the executable <target>-<version>; --full adds go test -json with coverage, go vet and gofmt -l. Dependencies use Go's module cache in the user's Go environment (not isolated per project). Evidence: fresh-checkout qualification.

The host coordinator selects declared targets and their dependency closure, prepares verified configured tools, asks each builder for its native build contract, and executes one shared task graph into one evidence bundle. Before preparation, host execution and --plan share logical selection, prerequisite/hook expansion and cycle validation. The executable host plan retains those dependency edges; the shared scheduler runs independent targets concurrently up to the resolved build.jobs ceiling. Build YAML depends_on gates consumers on the producer's selected stages. A failed dependency blocks its consumers while unrelated targets may finish. Stages within one target remain ordered to protect their shared native workspace. It does not claim process/network isolation or production eligibility. Explicit --isolated retains the isolated path and its existing tool-identity admission limits. Native and captured builds use the same executable-action description and shared operation/hook/report composition. Native artifact locations remain machine-local collection bindings to the plan's logical outputs. This changes no executor selection or fast/full default: native build commands retain their own lifecycle, including Maven tests within verify. Internal action boundaries do not imply a separate native invocation for each module or more precise cache inputs. Required reports and successful collection still gate artifacts; private workspaces alone do not establish enforcement. See task composition. Native support includes Cargo, Maven reactors producing jars, single-binary Go applications, explicit npm dist applications, and pip pyproject wheel distributions. Other Node/Python profiles retain the existing isolated path and its admission limits. npm uses npm ci for declared dependencies and requires a lockfile; pip uses its native PEP 517 wheel builder, including build-backend acquisition. Offline adds npm offline/pip no-index behavior and may fail when native prerequisites are unavailable. CPython is provisioned as a managed tool (Python installation); pip is the one bundled with it. pip performs build-backend acquisition during its wheel command; this is visible native preparation output, not a separate Oyzu dependency graph. Host wheels are distribution artifacts, not a bundled runnable Python application. First functional proof: run oyzu build from examples/tasks/grouped-targets/project without root overrides, produce the Python wheel and Node dist directory in one dist/manifest.json, then validate the bundle with oyzu inspect dist. Target selection, failure handling and a repeated invocation close the remaining functional checks. Broader native profiles remain separate follow-ups. Native builds now use private target workspaces and explicit artifact transfer. An ordering edge alone does not copy files. Additional shared-source inputs currently require the native host path. Windows verification: the grouped API/web build and oyzu inspect dist succeeded with both artifacts. python tooling/test-native-multi-build.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> verifies real npm multi-target builds, a selected target, repeated publication, missing-fresh-output rejection and a native child failure that blocks dependent tasks. The concurrency proof uses a two-process rendezvous, and the dependency proof checks producer completion before consumer execution. Native executable filename collisions are rejected before build actions. These checks do not qualify full-quality dependency availability for every ecosystem.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/project-environments.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every Oyzu build includes the mise library integration. Build with Rust 1.95 using cargo build --locked --bins; no integration feature flag exists. This page describes the experimental environment implementation, not a production-qualified release. Its scoped lifecycle checks passed on Windows PowerShell and Linux/macOS Bash and Zsh. See implementation status for measured results. The opt-in OCI session prototype adds Unix launch shims for provisioned Helm/BuildKit clients. Activation itself does not contact its agent; the native invocation requests a session using its current context.

An environment-only project needs no tools, lock, install or account. Shell activation and oyzu exec apply its environment after the folder is trusted; explicit project tasks and builds always apply it: [env] APP_MODE = "development" _.path = ["./bin", "./node_modules/.bin"] The array prepends directories in order. To append as well, use this alternative: [env] _.path = { prepend = ["./bin"], append = ["./scripts"] } The reserved env._ table is metadata, never an exported variable. Values and paths are literal: no variable expansion, scripts, dotenv discovery or command substitution. Plain env.PATH assignments are rejected with a migration message. Relative paths belong to the file declaring them, including local/profile files. They do not change when you enter a subdirectory. Missing directories are allowed. Empty entries, NUL, unknown controls and an embedded host PATH separator are errors. Use "." explicitly for the declaring directory. Normal configuration precedence applies. Each winning _.path declaration replaces the entire inherited control; [] clears project additions. Arrays preserve order. Selected tool shims precede project prepends, inherited PATH, then project appends. Existing occurrences are preserved rather than claimed as project-owned insertions. Projects within Git use the repository root unless --root is explicit. Outside Git, the outermost applicable ancestor Oyzu configuration establishes the root. Nested files affect only their subtree. Installed tools live in the shared user store, independently of the project owning the configuration and lock. Activation can select an explicit store with --store; relative store paths resolve against the invocation directory. Use the same store for installation and activation. Relative parent components such as ../tools are normalized lexically on every host before the store's existing no-follow filesystem checks; normalization does not create directories or relax symlink/reparse-point validation. Development tasks can select that store with oyzu run <task> --store <path>. The path follows the same invocation-directory resolution as build and install, and applies to the whole task sequence, including hooks and prerequisites. Tasks verify installed selections; this option does not install missing tools or fall back to another store. Preparation failures retain their original error and causes; shared stderr diagnostics give recovery guidance without replacing the error code. oyzu run list --store <path> remains discovery-only and does not open or create the store. Place task arguments after --; a --store after that separator is forwarded to the task instead.

In PowerShell 7.5+: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression Set-Location ./project-a Set-Location ../project-b oyzu deactivate In Bash or Zsh: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # substitute zsh for Zsh cd ./project-a cd ../project-b oyzu deactivate Activation can start outside any project. Directory hooks apply before the next command; configuration edits refresh at the next hook. Call _oyzu_hook to refresh explicitly in an activated shell. Hooks never install tools, run tasks or access the network. Tools declared in [tools] must already have a usable frozen selection. Profile installation is explicit: oyzu shell install SHELL --profile-path PATH. Removing that profile block changes future loads; deactivate the current session separately. See the profile instructions. Each activated terminal owns its state. A nested shell can call activate to obtain its own record and change projects without modifying its parent's record. Deactivation restores its inherited baseline. No shared global tool selection is changed.

Switching first reverses the prior project delta. A scalar restores only when it still equals Oyzu's applied value; user edits and deletions are preserved. A new project's explicit assignment temporarily overrides that edited baseline, which is restored afterward. Empty strings and absent variables remain distinct. Explicit removals use the existing configuration control: [overrides] remove = ["env.APP_MODE"] The variable is unset for that project and restored on unload if the user has not changed it. PATH restoration preserves unrelated additions and removes owned unique entries even after reordering. Ambiguous duplicate edits are retained with a diagnostic. Invalid configuration or unavailable required selection unloads the previous project's changes and reports OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=unavailable. Fix the configuration or explicitly install/update tools; the next hook retries. No failing project is partially applied. A usable environment reports ready. Managed environments and development secret references remain unsupported in this milestone and fail explicitly. Hooks do not authenticate, refresh credentials or fall back around authorization. Applying project/local literal values through activation, hooks, shims or exec requires folder trust, because shells, loaders and interpreters can execute the contents of environment variables.

Review the checkout's environment settings, then run oyzu trust [path]. With no path, this trusts the current project's root. oyzu trust --revoke [path] removes the record; oyzu trust --list lists records. Every form supports --json and human output. Trust is keyed by the canonical root folder, including resolution of symbolic links, and survives edits to oyzu.toml. It never writes into the checkout or contacts a service. Records live under trusted-projects in the native user state directory. Untrusted folders never prompt or block tool selection: activation still exposes the tools but skips project/local [env], env._.path, and their removals. User/global environment values remain effective. Prompt hooks, shims, exec and one-shot env --shell use the same rule. A short stderr hint names oyzu trust once per invocation, or once per activated shell session. run, build, build planning and the build configuration digest always include project/local env and PATH settings under normal configuration precedence, regardless of folder trust. These commands explicitly execute or plan the repo's declared code and must agree with CI. config inspection also retains the configured environment. User/global or administrative configuration can set [trust] enabled = false to disable the check, or parents = ["/absolute/projects"] to trust projects beneath selected canonical parent folders (for example E:\\CodexData\\projects on Windows). The default is enabled with no trusted parents. Project/local files cannot set these controls. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=false disables the check for an invocation; true enables it and overrides ordinary files. CI context is automatically trusted, including a true CI marker; platform executors run in that CI context. Local coding agents receive no exemption. Revocation removes only the explicit record: a parent rule, disabled check or CI exemption can still trust the folder. This changes earlier literal-environment behavior. Trust existing checkouts once, or configure their parent directory in user scope. Dedicated regression coverage tests scope rejection and the compiled CLI trust lifecycle; Windows native state and real shell qualification still require running the checks on that host.

oyzu env displays configuration sources, effective variable names and selected executables in separate tables. Names such as CARGO_HOME and cargo-llvm-cov are preserved literally. Configuration sources include env._.path, which is PATH metadata rather than a separate exported variable, and identify the winning source and profile from the resolved cascade (including oyzu.local.toml). Ordinary values are visible in human and JSON inspection. Credential-like names (including token, secret, password, API key, authentication and private-key names) and values rejected by the shared diagnostic sanitizer remain redacted. This is heuristic protection, not secret discovery: do not put secrets in innocuously named literal variables. Configuration/log inspection retains its separate, conservative redaction contract. Human output lists PATH entries in search order and removes Windows extended-path prefixes from displayed source paths. Tool-provided variables and inherited PATH also contribute to the composed environment. Inspection does not modify the calling shell. In an untrusted folder, oyzu env still shows configured values and provenance, with project entries marked skipped until trusted for activation, hooks, shims and exec. The displayed PATH describes the configured composition, including those entries; it is not a claim that activation has applied it. oyzu env --json lists inspected environment values and selected commands, with configuration provenance in the configuration array. projectEnvironmentSkipped reports whether shell/exec use withholds project environment, and affected configuration rows carry the same skipped until trusted status as human output. To apply directory changes in an existing PowerShell session, run oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. Then where.exe oyzu includes the project-local executable before the bootstrap if env._.path contains its directory. Leaving the project restores the prior PATH. For future shells, use the explicit shell profile installation. On Windows, directories Oyzu adds to PATH use ordinary drive or UNC notation, not the \\?\ prefixes used by internal filesystem canonicalization. Inherited PATH entries retain their original spelling for restoration. Windows PowerShell 5.1 can apply the initial activation, but the upstream directory-change hook requires PowerShell 7 or newer; use a supported PowerShell version for automatic switching (including the empty-variable requirement noted below). oyzu exec -- /absolute/path/to/program applies the trust-filtered environment, including unsets, to a child without changing the caller. Bare commands retain the existing declared-tool requirement. oyzu env --shell SHELL emits one-shot changes without installing lifecycle hooks; use activate for automatic rollback. PATH metadata does not become a task environment variable or a hermetic build input. The existing build/task contracts still own their explicit execution environments.

The repository's .oyzu/bin PATH declaration supports the in-development native CLI bootstrap workflow. Environment activation alone does not prove successful native compilation or repeated self-replacement. The activation wrapper dispatches ordinary CLI commands to the first oyzu application on the active PATH, falling back to the activating executable when none is found. Environment hooks and shell lifecycle commands retain the activating executable. This permits a successful local build to take over ordinary commands without reinstalling activation. The PowerShell lifecycle fixture verified this dispatch on Windows with the compiled limited-debug CLI on 2026-10-03. Native self-build and promotion remain separately unverified. Run python tooling/test-project-environments.py --cli PATH --shell pwsh or select bash/zsh. The fixture exercises real shell entry/switch/leave, nested scopes, unset/restore, config refresh, failure cleanup and child-session independence. It provisions no tools and checks that no project lock or tool store was created. The native CI workflow also compares ordinary and no-default-features command help. The intended shell matrix is Bash on Linux/macOS, Zsh on Linux/macOS and PowerShell 7.5+ where available. PowerShell 7.5 introduced support for preserving empty environment values; earlier versions cannot satisfy this environment contract (Microsoft documentation). Evidence is recorded separately; a test definition is not proof that every host passed. Additional shells, managed/secret integration, general shim expansion, active-installation retention, crash recovery, stress testing and performance tuning remain outside this environment milestone.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/remote-runs.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental client. oyzu build --remote and oyzu run <task> --remote implement the CLI side of the draft remote runs contract (design page). They are verified against a scripted local server and the contract's mock; no platform service implements the contract yet, so they are not qualified against one.

--remote runs the same invocation on a platform pool instead of this machine: the pool checks out the exact pushed commit, runs oyzu build or oyzu run <task> there with full checks in isolation, and streams the output back. The CLI follows it to the end and exits with the remote exit code. Everything else Oyzu does stays local and works without an account; --remote is the optional platform path.

A Git checkout whose HEAD is pushed to a github.com repository linked to a project in your platform account. git must be on PATH. platform.url and platform.account in user/global, machine or administrative configuration. Project/local scope is rejected with a diagnostic naming the key: oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments CI can supply OYZU_PLATFORM_URL and OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT through the configuration contract. These invocation sources override ordinary files and remain subject to administrative constraints. A checkout cannot redirect a developer's platform credential, even when its environment is trusted. An access token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Interactive login from the authentication contract is not implemented yet; the token is a credential, so it is read from the environment and never from a configuration file.

Command Runs remotely oyzu build --remote Every target oyzu build cli web --remote Targets cli and web (and what they depend on) oyzu build --affected origin/main --remote Targets affected since the merge base of origin/main and HEAD oyzu run policy-check --remote Task policy-check (target:task also works) … --remote --download out The same, then downloads every output into out/ oyzu build --remote --plan previews a remote build locally without creating a run; see planning a remote run. The CLI resolves the repository from the current branch's remote (else origin), the full HEAD commit and the checked-out branch ref. For --affected it sends the full merge-base commit, never a local ref name.

Text mode uses the same linear view as a local build. Each log line the pool streams is attributed to the target or task that wrote it (scope in the contract), so task starts, native output and task results look like local ones. The runner's own lines (checkout, start, finish) appear under runner. The receipt on stdout leads with the outcome, then the run id, commit, project, Oyzu version, portal link when there is one, and the outputs the run produced: ✓ Remote build succeeded Run 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 Commit 3f2a9c1d4b5e (main) Project oyzu/platform Oyzu 0.9.0 Outputs manifest dist/manifest.json 4.0 KiB sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaa report dist/cli/reports/junit.xml 2.0 KiB sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbb Use --download <DIR> to fetch outputs; nothing was written locally. With --json, stderr carries the same structured events a local build emits (output events keep the remote scope as operationId) and stdout carries one remote-run record: run (the final run resource), result (state, exit code, reason and outputs), downloads (path, digest, local file) and cancelled. The record also contains invocationId, the exact submission body (repository, commit and selection), observation and a cancellation object. After a run has been created, failure to follow or retrieve its result produces an unknown outcome with the last observed run state/time and log position; it does not assert failed remote execution or start local work. The last run-resource state can predate subsequent scoped task log events. Known log gaps remain explicit in the result even after a connection recovers. Complete observation means the client received terminal records, not that every log entry or required artifact transfer is complete. Bounded retry notices describe observation loss and recovery. Submission, observation and requested artifact transfer are distinct phases. The current public contract supplies queued/running/final states and scoped task lifecycles; worker identity, assignment and detailed worker preparation/transfer telemetry are unavailable and are not inferred from illustrative studies.

Remote outcome Exit code Succeeded 0 Oyzu exited non-zero on the pool That exit code Failed before Oyzu ran, skipped, cancelled, timed out, or an unknown state 1 Refused before or while creating the run (configuration, Git, platform problem) 2 Interrupted with Ctrl-C 130 An unknown remote outcome after submission exits non-zero (1); an interrupt retains exit 130. Use the supplied Web link, or check the run ID with the platform operator when no link was supplied, before starting a replacement run. Reattachment and CLI retrieval of a previous remote run are not implemented.

The first Ctrl-C asks the platform to cancel the run and keeps following its log while the pool stops it; a second Ctrl-C exits at once with 130. The observer keeps following beyond the local cleanup grace period so it can retain the execution owner's confirmed outcome. Cancelling is retry-safe, so a cancel that races the run's own finish is harmless. There is no confirmation prompt, so cancelling works the same in CI. cancelled records that this invocation requested cancellation. It is not confirmation that execution stopped. cancellation.requested, acknowledged and confirmed expose separate facts; confirmation follows a terminal cancelled result. A finished-run conflict is followed to its actual outcome. The receipt preserves pending or unknown cancellation and any known log gaps. Assigned native workers use the same cooperative interruption lifetime as a local captured build. A running cancellation acknowledgement requires the execution owner's normal process wait and fresh finalized native build record; revoking a lease or receiving a success response alone is insufficient. Forced or unconfirmed stops remain explicit failures. The real Linux service/worker proof passed cancellation during the shared native action: the observer retained all three cancellation facts and exited 130 after confirmed cleanup. A second real run preserved an already accepted shared contribution while stopping API and preventing the final bundle from starting; see the distributed qualification record. resultAvailable distinguishes a fetched result from a partial observation. When the final run resource is already confirmed, losing access to its result retains that execution outcome and identifies unavailable metadata/outputs. The invocation still fails if requested observation cannot complete. Last-observed timestamps advance on actual responses; elapsed waiting is not execution progress.

Outputs are listed by digest and never written into dist/. --download <DIR> fetches each one through the platform's short-lived download link, which receives no platform credential, verifies its SHA-256 digest before writing, and writes it at its recorded path under DIR. A path that would leave DIR is refused. For accepted native split builds, these are the manifest, artifacts and required reports. The output projection excludes the private admitted plan, execution envelope and logs; it is not a complete local build bundle for oyzu inspect. The existing run log view retains remote observation separately. Native contribution validation precedes final platform success; downloaded file digests are checked again by the client. Reported native success does not guarantee platform acceptance. If the complete transferred contribution cannot be verified, the run fails with CONTRIBUTION_UNVERIFIED and no accepted outputs. This does not turn successful native actions into failed tests or grant permission to replay their commands. Inspect the run's diagnostic and retained native evidence before retrying. The result must contain an outputs array, including an empty array when there are no outputs. Every output supplies its kind (manifest, report or artifact), media type, nonnegative size, path and digest. A missing or malformed array or missing output metadata fails with REMOTE_RESPONSE_INVALID before downloads start, in human and JSON modes, even when the platform reports that the run succeeded. Check the platform's result and client compatibility; the remote run itself is not restarted.

Refusals never fall back to a local build. Platform problems keep their stable code with a REMOTE_ prefix and the platform request id, for example REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED (set a current token), REMOTE_REPOSITORY_NOT_LINKED, REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_FOUND (push first) and REMOTE_VALIDATION_FAILED. Local checks fail before any request: REMOTE_NOT_CONFIGURED, REMOTE_NOT_A_CHECKOUT, REMOTE_REPOSITORY_UNSUPPORTED (not github.com), REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED (HEAD is on no branch of the remote) and REMOTE_AFFECTED_BASE_INVALID. Uncommitted changes produce a warning: they are not part of the run. Requests that fail in transport or answer 503 are retried up to five times with backoff, honoring Retry-After. Creation is retried under the same Idempotency-Key, so a retry never starts a second run. Logs are followed with 30-second long polls over plain HTTPS and resume from the last cursor, so the client works through proxies (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE) with outbound access alone.

The token is sent only to platform.url as a bearer credential. platform.url must be HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host, for local development against a mock. Run ids and digests from the platform are validated before they are used in a URL or a file name, and log text is escaped before it reaches the terminal like local child output.

The #479 implementation candidate connects internal admitted native preparation and assigned-plan verification separately from public read-only preview. This has passed the connected real-service flow on Linux, including distinct API/Web workers, an independent whole-build artifact/report comparison, cancellation, retained-byte upload retry, safe worker replacement, coupled prerequisites and required output/report/contribution refusals without implicit replay. The agreed finite cases and exact qualification limits are recorded in distributed build completion. No interactive login; the token comes from OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. GitHub repositories on github.com only, matching the contract's github provider. Task arguments (-- args) are not supported remotely. --detach, listing runs and re-attaching to a run are not implemented. Broader platform/host qualification remains incomplete; see the linked distributed qualification record and RUNS-08/RUNS-09 in the design page.

oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked --test integration remote_runs: the compiled CLI against a scripted server for a successful build with scoped log replay and verified download, a failing task's exit code and JSON event stream, an expired token and an unpushed HEAD. python tooling/check-runs-contract.py: the contract and its mock, including scoped log entries. python tooling/test-remote-cli.py --cli <compiled-oyzu>: the compiled CLI against the contract mock end to end.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-commands.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: implemented for the tools Oyzu admits today; the design is the accepted OEP-0021 tool commands proposal (design accepted 2026-10-07; implementation experimental). Syntax, error codes and the choices listed under accepted choices may still change. Platforms: developed and verified on Linux x86-64 only; Windows and macOS are unverified (see verification). These commands change what a scope requires ([tools] in configuration) and what it has locked (oyzu.lock) together, and inspect the result. They use the existing providers: node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm, rust, the Cargo helpers cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov, and, experimentally, registry packages written aqua:<owner>/<repo> (see the aqua: backend) or github:<owner>/<repo> (see the github: backend). No account is needed. oyzu install go@1.26 # this project: declare, lock, install oyzu install -g node@22 # your user configuration, all projects oyzu install go # declared: ensure installed; undeclared: go@latest oyzu update go # newer version within the requirement; config untouched oyzu uninstall go # remove the project declaration and lock entry oyzu tools current # what is in effect here oyzu tools list # what is in the store, and what references it oyzu tools versions go # what could be installed oyzu tools info go # provider, verification, eligibility
documents.s: Tool commands: install, update, uninstall and inspection

documents.t: oyzu pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 edits the project's [tools] requests and locks their exact archives for the configured platforms in one transaction. All archive providers use this path, including Python, Maven, Gradle, npm and pnpm. --dry-run previews the result without writing. Explicit specs cannot be combined with --refresh or --offline; bare oyzu pin retains discovery-driven pinning, refresh and offline behavior. Normal configuration precedence and policy still apply, and overridden requests fail without changing files. The result uses the shared declaration presentation: requested/selected versions, covered and unavailable platforms, configuration path and lock path. oyzu --json pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 returns the same facts with status: "pinned". Pinning does not install payloads or prepare shims. Publisher metadata acquisition may verify archive bytes where its checksum format requires conversion; indexed pinning reads the index/catalog only (Rust also reads the approved manifest). Run oyzu install --frozen afterward to install. The defaults include linux/arm64/gnu; locks can carry it on any host. An unavailable provider/platform is omitted and reported. macOS amd64 and musl are not added to installation support. See implementation status for explicit-spec and ARM64 verification results.

Flag Configuration written Lock none, inside a project project oyzu.toml (created if absent) project oyzu.lock -g, --global the user configuration file (OYZU_USER_CONFIG or the native location) the oyzu.lock beside it --local oyzu.local.toml project oyzu.lock --profile NAME (global option) that profile's [profiles.NAME.tools] as above A project is --root, or the workspace root when it holds oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml, build.yaml or a Git marker. Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT and writes nothing; it never guesses. --global and --local conflict. A command acts on the selected scope only and prints a note when the same tool is declared elsewhere. -g ignores project files entirely, including when run inside a project.

install with no arguments installs everything declared in the effective configuration (--frozen, --offline, --update). oyzu install --global installs the global selection independently of the current project, using the user configuration and its sibling oyzu.lock. It accepts the same frozen, offline, update and store controls; it never edits project declarations or locks. For example, oyzu install --global --frozen --offline restores a previously locked global selection using locally available installation or acquisition data. Missing locks fail with TOOL_LOCK_MISSING; an offline installation still requires the needed cached data. With specs: A spec is [provider:]name[@version], split at the last @. go@1.26 is a prefix, go@1.26.8 is exact, go@latest is the newest eligible version, and go alone keeps a declared requirement (ensuring it is installed) or takes latest when undeclared. Several specs are applied together or not at all. Naming a tool twice is TOOL_SPEC_INVALID. Configuration stores what you typed ("1.26"); the lock stores the exact version. Core tools (node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, rust) are written under the name you typed; other tools (cargo-nextest) are written under their canonical ID ("cargo:cargo-nextest") so a later alias change cannot alter the file. An existing declaration keeps its spelling. Existing TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED and TOOL_ALIAS_AMBIGUOUS behavior is preserved, and an ambiguous bare name fails listing the exact retry spellings. Order of operations: parse specs, evaluate tools.allowed, resolve every platform in the default set (Linux x64, macOS arm64, Windows x64 for archive tools; tools.platforms overrides), install only the host archive, then publish configuration and lock in one journaled transaction. Any failure leaves both files unchanged. Concurrent edits fail with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. Declared tools of the same lock that are not yet in the portable lock layer are resolved in the same run, keeping the exact version they already had, and are installed too, so the whole selection remains consistent. Replacing a requirement reports Replaced "1.25" (1.25.9) -> "1.26" (1.26.8) and reuses an installation already in the store. --dry-run resolves (reading publisher catalogs) and reports versions, files and platforms; it downloads no archive and writes nothing. Specs with --frozen, --offline or --update fail with TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT before any project, configuration or network access, as do --dry-run and --local without specs. Archive tools and Rust-family tools resolve through different contracts; one command cannot mix them (TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT: run two commands). Result (human, then the shape of --json: tools[] with tool, key, request, version, previous, status, platforms, otherScopes; plus configuration, lock, scope, store): ✓ Installed go 1.26.8 Declared "1.26" in ./oyzu.toml (project) Locked in ./oyzu.lock for 3 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc)

install recipe:owner/name@version --artifact-set FILE [--artifact-set-digest sha256:D] supplies the tool from a resolved artifact set instead of a built-in provider, and tools info … --artifact-set shows the same eligibility without side effects. --dry-run reports eligibility only. Details, output and limits are in artifact sets; the flags are provisional, apply to the project scope only (-g/--local fail TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT) and the install downloads and verifies the artifact and writes the lock, but does not yet extract or activate a recipe tool. install --frozen replays locked recipe: tools from the lock alone.

update [TOOL...] re-resolves within the existing requirement, locks the result for all platforms, installs the host selection and never edits configuration. No arguments updates every tool of the selected scope. It takes names, not versions. install --update remains as a deprecated alias with its old behavior (all scopes). A tool still missing from the portable layer is migrated, keeping its version. Hand-edited removals are not pruned from the lock.

uninstall TOOL... removes the declaration (comments elsewhere in the file are kept) and every lock record for the tool at the selected scope, in one transaction. Shared payloads are never deleted: they remain in tools list as unreferenced. A tool not declared at that scope fails with TOOL_NOT_DECLARED and names the scope that does declare it. --dry-run writes nothing.

All inspection is read-only, performs no installation, never re-hashes installed payloads (installs are verified once, then trusted) and prints the store path. tools current [-g] [--all] [--details]: one row per effective tool with the requested and selected versions, scope and status. --global shows only global declarations; --all adds declarations a more specific scope overrides. Statuses: ok, not installed (locked but absent from the store), blocked (tools.allowed, naming the rule), stale lock (no lock, no matching entry, or no entry for this platform or provider), ambiguous (conflicting lock records or names), and deprecated (reserved; no provider reports it yet). tools list: installations in the store with size and what references each: global (the user lock), project (this project's lock) or unreferenced. Other projects are not indexed, so an installation reported unreferenced may be used elsewhere. tools versions TOOL: selectable versions, newest first, from the publisher's catalog, or from the tool index when one is configured and lists the package (which also works offline from its cached copy). Otherwise requires network (TOOL_OFFLINE with --offline). Pre-release, snapshot and nightly versions are not offered by the adapters, so excluded is always empty today; a tool blocked by tools.allowed reports why. Rust and Cargo helpers have no catalog (TOOL_VERSIONS_UNSUPPORTED). tools info TOOL: provider, accepted names, commands, platforms, verification, eligibility, declarations by scope and current state. tools check --catalog and tools migrate [--write]: check declarations against the tool index, and move mise.toml tools and aqua: ids to Oyzu names; see the tool index reference.

Code Meaning TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Unparseable spec, empty version, duplicate tool TOOL_NO_PROJECT Project scope outside a project; use --global TOOL_NOT_DECLARED uninstall/update of a tool the scope does not declare TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT Specs with --frozen/--offline/--update; spec-only flags without specs; mixed resolution contracts; a declaration overridden in this invocation CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED tools.allowed excludes the tool; names the rule, nothing written TOOL_ALIAS_*, TOOL_LOCK_*, PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT Existing codes, unchanged An interrupted configuration/lock publication is recovered before reading configuration when retrying oyzu install, oyzu update or oyzu uninstall. Install recovery precedes configuration preflight and artifact-set replay, including plain, --frozen, --offline, spec and artifact-set forms. Offline configuration reads also use the offline session policy. oyzu pin also recovers it. Read-only commands report PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED with the affected directory and a recovery command. Unexpected external edits stop recovery with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT; the journal remains for investigation. Configuration and lock readers capture one consistent pair under the shared edit lock, then release it before acquiring or launching tools. A concurrent first edit or a change while capturing additional targets reports CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT; retry the command. Recipe-staleness errors identify the actual tool, version and lock path. Use oyzu pin --refresh to refresh recipes while retaining selected versions, then oyzu install to materialize them. Tool-preparation failures identify the tool, requested or pinned version, store path and recovery command. Windows paths in these diagnostics use the plain C:\... or \\server\share\... form in both human and JSON output; the extended \\?\ prefix remains an internal filesystem detail. Unix diagnostic paths are unchanged.

Recorded in the proposal's decision record (accepted 2026-10-07): no provider prefix beyond canonical IDs; core tools stored as typed; no allow-list patterns; no prerelease flag; tools versions has no offline source; no project index; bare oyzu tools unchanged. A platform for which the provider publishes no artifact for the requested version is omitted from the lock and reported as unavailable (a warning in the human view, unavailablePlatforms in --json). The other platforms lock and the host installs normally; selecting the unavailable platform fails. Example: oyzu install node@14 locks Linux and Windows only, because Node 14 has no macOS arm64 build. This applies when a tool is first declared or re-declared with a new request, and only for the Node, Go and JDK catalogs; an update re-resolves only the platforms already locked, and a tool with no artifact on any platform fails. Any other resolution failure (for example a missing checksum file) still fails the command.

Linux only verified. Mixed archive and Rust-family specs need separate commands. Installing one tool also installs the other declared tools of its lock group. Config and lock publication is journaled, with recovery as described above. Managed (enrolled) mode is rejected as for the other tool commands.
tooling/test-tool-commands.py drives the compiled CLI against real Go and Node downloads; tests/integration/tool_commands.rs covers the no-download cases. See the qualification record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-management-development.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Node, Go and Rust installation use Oyzu configuration, internal tool mechanics, version-1 locks and the shared installation store. The mise application and fork are not runtime dependencies. Adapted code retains its upstream notices. This remains development functionality, not a distribution-qualified release. All archive providers now share indexed pin/install governance, including npm and pnpm. Native host support includes Linux ARM64 GNU alongside Linux amd64 GNU, macOS arm64 and Windows amd64 MSVC. Node ARM64 archives use the vendor's linux-arm64 spelling. Historical proofs below do not establish native ARM64 qualification. See implementation status for current verification. See provider coverage, indexed Rust and pin declarations. Build with Rust 1.95 or newer using cargo build --locked --bins. A private Oyzu worker installs Rust from frozen inputs; Node and Go use internal metadata and archive mechanics through the acquisition broker. No separate mise executable is used. The provider contract now has an Oyzu-owned identity. Unreleased locks from the retired adapter must be regenerated with oyzu pin --refresh, followed by oyzu install. There is no legacy compatibility reader or receipt relabeling; existing payloads are retained. See provider identity.

Pin output separates managed tool requirements from executor prerequisites. Inventory JSON includes category (managed-tool, executor-prerequisite or constraint); category does not claim provider support or installed availability. Pinning records managed resolutions, not observed machine paths or SDK inventory. Installation remains limited to admitted tool providers and never installs OS components. Native project dependencies retain their native manifest/lock owner. See native build readiness and the design boundary. Native npm execution uses the selected Node installation's bundled npm/npx through Oyzu's verified execution environment. No aube installer or mise application is embedded. Native npm retains its own registry, authentication and cache semantics; Oyzu controls prerequisite selection, execution and evidence. Bundled commands need no separate tool declaration. Explicit npm/pnpm releases use their own providers; selecting npm overrides Node's bundled copy. Python similarly exposes its interpreter aliases and bundled pip through the selected Python, including Windows module-only layouts. Developer commands use the shared composed-PATH lookup, including host commands; controlled builds retain their separate admission rules. Mise's aube-dependent Node workspace task provider is omitted; Oyzu owns its own task discovery and execution.

The shared-store/portable-lock realignment is in progress. Resolution records now contain request facts and recipe roots without scope/profile labels. Rust lookup uses version, execution platform and required components and selects the smallest pinned recipe that contains them; incomparable matching recipes fail with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS. A cross target's request includes its target-platform standard library. Configuration continues to own profile and directory precedence. Installation records are also keyed by effective requests, and store leases consume an exact selection digest rather than a directory or profile. Schema version remains 1. Earlier development records containing scope/profile or the obsolete requirements inventory are rejected by the strict decoder rather than silently reused. Regenerate these unreleased locks with the current CLI; retain existing payloads until reuse is verified. User-origin requirements use the lock beside the user configuration file; project-origin requirements use the project lock. An arbitrary invocation directory does not acquire a lock for user defaults. A project overriding one tool retains unrelated user defaults. Configuration chooses the owner before lock matching; owner labels and paths are not persisted in portable records. OYZU_USER_CONFIG can select an absolute user configuration file without changing machine policy locations; see the configuration reference.

oyzu tools list oyzu tools current oyzu tools current --details oyzu tools current --json oyzu which node tools list reads installation receipts in the selected store independently of project configuration. tools current resolves effective configuration and its locks, showing selected versions, missing installations, configuration provenance and component purposes. Both support --details for full locations, identities and cross-compilation targets, --store, and the global --json flag. Inspection does not install tools, update locks or acquire over the network. A nonexistent store remains nonexistent. Human output uses a concise aligned summary with configuration filenames; --details includes full paths. JSON always retains the complete structured records. These inventory commands report stored metadata, not freshly verified payload integrity. which and execution use verified installation selections and can therefore reject an installation whose receipt was visible in inventory. A missing lock is reported as stale lock; stale, ambiguous or incompatible locked selections fail rather than selecting an unrelated installed version. Install the declared selection explicitly to resolve missing payloads. Declaring, updating and removing tools and browsing versions are covered by tool commands, which also defines the current status words (ok, not installed, blocked, deprecated, stale lock, ambiguous); pruning remains separate follow-up work. Successful installation output reports installed or reused for each selected tool, its version and Rust components. Reuse still verifies the selected payload; these result labels do not change lock selection or acquisition. Errors retain their failure exit status and do not produce a successful installation summary. Native installer diagnostics use the shared invocation logger on stderr, including structured records under --json; stdout remains the command result. Use oyzu build --store <path> when building with a store selected by oyzu install --store <path>. Omitting the override always selects the shared user store, not a store remembered from an earlier command. See local builds.

Create oyzu.toml at the workspace root: [tools] node = "22.15.0" [env] APP_MODE = "development" Then run the Oyzu binary: oyzu install oyzu install --frozen oyzu install --frozen --offline oyzu which node oyzu env --json oyzu exec -- node --version oyzu exec -- node -e 'console.log(process.env.APP_MODE)' The shell quoting in the last example is suitable for Bash and PowerShell. -C DIRECTORY, explicit root and profile selection use the existing configuration resolver. Installation supports Node, Go and Rust selections at the workspace root. The Node selector is interpreted by the extracted metadata library against the actual Node catalog. Existing locks retain the exact version unless an update is explicitly requested. If a maintained adapter changes an installation layout (for example, adding the bundled npm entrypoint to Node), ordinary or frozen reuse reports TOOL_LAYOUT_STALE. Run oyzu install --update node to explicitly rebuild the selected layout from verified archive inputs. This uses the normal online update contract: version constraints still apply and metadata refresh requires access. Repinning alone does not replace an existing installation. The replacement is staged and verified before publication; the older installation and its receipt remain intact, including for existing leases. Subsequent selection prefers the currently admitted layout and still verifies its payload. Updating a different tool does not authorize changing Node's layout. Duplicate equally eligible receipts remain an ambiguity error. No schema migration or receipt relabeling is performed. Tool names are resolved locally from the admitted adapter definitions, with upstream alias provenance retained in the extracted registry. Name resolution does not start a backend worker, inspect an installation or access the network. Version/catalog resolution and acquisition still use their existing backend and verification contracts. For the currently admitted backends, node and "oyzu:node" identify the same tool, as do go and "oyzu:go", and rust and "oyzu:rust". Oyzu's own providers were named core:<name> before 2026-10-10; core:node is still accepted as an input alias for oyzu:node (in configuration, commands and route scopes), but the lock and every report use oyzu: ids. Registry packages follow the same rule; see tool ids. Quote canonical TOML keys containing a colon. Changing only between these names preserves the normalized request identity and existing lock; it does not require installation or relocking. Defining both names for one tool fails with TOOL_ALIAS_AMBIGUOUS, even if their versions agree. Unknown registry names fail with TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED. This does not enable additional backends or make alias names executable commands: use node, go, cargo, rustc or rustdoc for exec. Selective updates accept the same registry names. Administrative tools.allowed values are compared through that same alias map; this setting remains admin-only. The real acceptance runner is python tooling/test-tool-aliases.py --cli PATH --workspace NODE_ACCEPTANCE_PATH; it reuses the two-version Node workspace above without changing its projects. Add --update for online canonical-name resolution. On a disposable root Linux host only, --disposable-linux-host temporarily creates an administrative policy to check both allowed-name spellings and denial; it refuses an existing policy and removes its own file afterwards. Linux offline replay with networking disabled and the separate online update passed on 2026-10-02. Native CI remains pending. After editing the Node requirement in TOML, run: oyzu install --update node oyzu exec -- node --version For a Node-only project, bare --update and --update oyzu:node select the same root. The command resolves through the Oyzu provider, prints the previous and proposed exact version, installs the result and then commits the lock using the existing compare-and-swap transaction. It never edits TOML. Ordinary install rejects changed requirements with TOOL_LOCK_STALE and an update remedy. --update conflicts with --frozen and --offline; unsupported tool names fail. A failed update leaves the previous lock intact. An unchanged resolution preserves lock bytes. A newly configured Node/Go project can reuse an exact installation even before it has its own installation lock. After backend version resolution, installation looks up the matching user-store receipt before downloading an archive to learn its size. It validates the layout and verifies the payload through the same publication/lease contract, then writes the project's portable lock. Version resolution can still require catalog metadata; this is distinct from downloading or extracting the tool again. Offline/frozen installation still requires pins. Updates operate on effective requests grouped by their configuration-owned lock. Replacing a request set preserves other request sets and platform distributions; conflicting acquisition facts for the same exact identity/platform fail rather than being overwritten. Other projects sharing the store keep their own locks and versions. Publication is atomic per lock owner, not across user and project locks together. Installation prepares the current host selection; it does not materialize every platform recorded in a portable lock. The default store is user-level: %LOCALAPPDATA%/Oyzu/tools on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/tools on macOS, and ${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/oyzu/tools on Linux (relative XDG values use the home fallback). On Windows, an absolute HOME different from the native profile selects <HOME>/AppData/Local/Oyzu/tools; unset HOME or use the normal profile to retain the native LocalAppData location. All default consumers resolve this location independently of the project directory. Explicit --store PATH overrides remain available for install, which, exec and environment commands; relative overrides resolve from the invocation directory. Use --store .oyzu/tools explicitly to inspect/reuse a previous project-local store. Existing contents are not automatically moved or deleted. Store routing is implemented; complete context-independent lock matching, automatic existing-content reuse and user-global selection remain under the active implementation brief. Installation requests metadata and the archive through Oyzu's existing HTTP host fetcher, using https://nodejs.org/dist/ unless an administrative connector route applies (see below). It checks the archive against Node's declared SHA-256, derives the layout from the extracted metadata library, stages and publishes the installation, then commits the lock through the existing lock-edit transaction. The lock explicitly records digest-only verification; it does not claim a verified publisher signature. An existing incompatible lock fails rather than being silently replaced. A failed installation does not publish a new lock. install --frozen requires an existing compatible lock and never resolves a new version. Both ordinary and frozen installs reuse an already installed selection after verifying its receipt and contents; this path needs no network and leaves the lock unchanged. If the installation is absent, Oyzu first verifies the cached archive against the locked digest and size, then restores the installed tree. Only a missing archive requires acquisition from the selected route; invalid cached content fails instead of silently downloading a replacement. install --offline forbids metadata and artifact networking. It requires an existing compatible lock and either a verified installation or its cached archive. Combine it with --frozen to explicitly prohibit lock edits. Missing locks or archives fail with an online-install remedy. Run ordinary install online to create the initial lock and acquire the required bytes. which node prints the selected receipt entrypoint. Trusted PATH overrides can choose another program during exec. Inspection shares read-only developer selection and verified installation lookup, makes no network request and does not install or launch anything. A missing installation fails instead of returning a system PATH executable. Without a compatible pin, inspection can reuse matching recorded installations; it never creates a lock. Developer exec composes configured tools with ordinary executable lookup on PATH. Missing configured tools install on invocation by default through Oyzu's existing acquisition, lock and receipt machinery. Compatible locked versions are retained; a new configured selection may publish oyzu.lock. This behavior is separate from controlled build admission: system PATH cannot satisfy a locked build requirement. See invocation controls. The selected installation leases remain held during native execution. Arguments, streams, cwd and native exit status pass through; no shell expression is inferred. exec also accepts an explicit absolute or relative executable path. It resolves relative paths against -C/the invocation directory and applies the same developer selection, configuration eligibility and environment. For example: oyzu exec -- ./bin/development-runner "argument with spaces" oyzu exec -- /usr/bin/python3 scripts/check.py On Windows, use a full executable path such as oyzu exec -- C:\Python313\python.exe scripts\check.py. Drive-relative paths such as C:python.exe are rejected as ambiguous. A program started this way can find the selected Node at the front of PATH; the explicit program itself is a requested development command, not a verified locked tool. This is ordinary development execution, not the hermetic build executor. Invoke an interpreter explicitly for scripts that need one. No implicit shell parsing is added. Bare commands use the composed PATH, including ordinary globally installed executables. Commands absent from PATH fail with COMMAND_NOT_FOUND. Explicit missing paths and directories fail lookup; invocation preparation may first install configured tools when automatic installation is enabled. which npm returns the bundled npm JavaScript entry point; exec npm and the npm shim launch it with the same verified Node interpreter. Managed execution and process-tree/signal supervision remain unfinished. Exercise the actual explicit-path flow against the retained two-project acceptance workspace with: python tooling/test-tool-exec.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH Linux amd64 passed this scenario with container networking disabled on 2026-10-02. Native Windows/macOS explicit-path execution acceptance remains pending in CI.

oyzu exec -- bash scripts/check.sh and oyzu exec -- sh scripts/check.sh use the same developer selection, composed PATH, tool environment and child-stream/exit contracts as other exec commands. Configured tools follow invocation install controls; Oyzu does not install the host shell or add implicit shell parsing. Linux/macOS resolve these shell names normally on PATH. Trusted project PATH prepends precede selected tool directories. On Windows, bare bash/sh select a native shell in this order: bash.exe/sh.exe on the composed PATH, excluding %SystemRoot%\System32 and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps WSL launchers/aliases. Git for Windows' bin\bash.exe/bin\sh.exe, derived from git.exe found on PATH under cmd, bin, mingw64\bin, mingw32\bin or usr\bin. Git\bin under %ProgramFiles% or %ProgramFiles(x86)%, then %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git\bin. If no native shell is found, the error describes the search and requires Git for Windows' shell. Make an existing Git installation discoverable or supply its explicit executable path. No WSL fallback occurs. Explicit paths still select exactly the requested executable. The host shell itself is not a locked tool. Git Bash/MSYS converts ordinary Windows PATH entries to its POSIX form on startup; Oyzu continues exporting ordinary drive paths, not verbatim \\?\ paths or a manually rewritten POSIX PATH. The same resolver serves host tasks, including shell-string tasks. tooling/test-tool-exec.py also checks bare bash/sh, argv tasks and shell-string tasks against the real pinned Node executable in its provisioned acceptance workspace. These additions still need desktop/CI execution on Windows, Linux and macOS; earlier explicit-path results do not establish this coverage.

A project can request both tools in the same TOML file: [tools] node = "22.15.0" go = "1.24.13" oyzu install oyzu which node oyzu which go oyzu exec -- node --version oyzu exec -- go version oyzu install --update node Installation resolves the configured roots, prepares missing installations and publishes one version-1 lock only after the complete selection is available. Existing content-addressed installations can be reused across single-tool and mixed projects. Failure leaves the previous lock intact; acquired cache entries may remain for reuse. --update node or --update oyzu:node resolves only Node and retains Go's exact record, version and artifact identity. The equivalent Go names preserve Node. Multiple update names select those roots; bare --update selects all configured roots. Adding a tool requires an update that includes it. Removing a tool from TOML requires bare --update. Changing an unselected request fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE; include that tool in the update or restore its requirement. The command never edits TOML. Unchanged requests/records retain their existing text through the lock-edit contract. For portable pins, updates refresh the selected tool's recipes for every platform already recorded for that request. Unselected recipes retain their identities; the host installation is verified before the candidate portable lock is committed. Exact requests and Node/Go ranges use the same provider selection rules as pinning. The candidate passes the same native-constraint and component validation as frozen execution; updates do not bypass that contract. Pinned Rust distribution inputs use 8 MiB HTTP range requests. Each request keeps the broker's 45-second deadline, source/redirect authorization and bounded retries; a progressing large download no longer has to fit into a single request deadline. The response ranges must be contiguous, match the requested offsets and lengths, and agree on the total size. The complete artifact must still match its locked SHA-256 before rustup can use it. The existing 256 MiB artifact and 1 GiB session byte limits include partial/failed transfer bytes as before. A server that ignores ranges may return a complete first response, still subject to the ordinary request timeout and byte limit. A full response after partial segments, inconsistent ranges or digest mismatch fails closed. No alternate source or unpinned download is used. Errors identify the pinned Rust input name without including upstream URLs or credentials. Other acquisition paths retain their existing request behavior.
